articles.title: Could these alternative homes be the future in a hotter Britain?
articles.summary: The Passivhaus standard is growing in popularity as UK homeowners adapt to hotter summer temperatures.
articles.body:
After five heatwaves and plenty of advice on how to stay safe in what is set to become the UK's hottest summer on record, many people continue to find it a challenge to stay cool - particularly in their homes.

This is perhaps no surprise. More than half of homes in the UK are already at risk of overheating and at current rates of climate change this will rise to 92% by 2050 if we do not adapt.

But in south London, on a 35C day, one 1960s ex-council house with no air-conditioning is managing to beat the heat.

Marion Baeli's home is one of many across the UK being adapted for warmer - maybe even 40C - British summers.

As well as being the homeowner, Baeli is an architect - and she compares her house to a well-insulated flask.

"You wouldn't put holes in your flask if you wanted to keep the ice in. You'd close the cap and make sure it is firmly twisted on. It's the same in this house."

When the BBC visit Baeli on the hottest day of this summer's fourth heatwave, her house is 10C cooler than outside.

"It feels like you have air-conditioning [inside the house] but you haven't. This is the beauty of the Passivhaus standard," she explains.

Passivhaus is an international building standard that was developed around 35 years ago in Germany. The concept is simple: design your home to keep the temperature constant at all times, by effectively sealing it against the elements.

It is estimated they consume up to 90% less energy than typical houses.

When the Baeli family moved in 10 years ago, their house had draughty PVC double-glazed windows with little insulation - they struggled to keep warm in the winter and overheated in the summer.

The most disruptive part of the retrofit work was carried out first, and included the insulation of shared walls, flooring and the roof.

The work also focused on getting rid of "thermal bridges" - which are parts of the home where heat is exchanged rapidly, such as where the insulation is broken up between rafters in your home.

Two years later, during the second phase of the works some cavity brick walls were replaced with "thinner, super-insulated" timber-framed walls, while new triple-glazed windows were installed to slow down the transfer of heat from outside.

With the house now air-tight, a ventilation system went in to ensure that the air inside the house was constantly kept fresh.

These measures work to prevent the temperature fluctuating inside the house - in winter and summer - so less energy is used.

In the colder months, one radiator is now sufficient to heat Baeli's four-bedroom home over three floor she says, because heat is not being lost.

Baeli estimates energy demand in her retrofitted house has gone down by 88%, giving her a yearly saving of nearly £750 on her bills.

But the Passivhaus Trust - for which Baeli is a non-executive director - acknowledges retrofitting your home to this standard is "expensive".

The total cost of the work Baeli carried out on her house was around £80,000, not including any additional costs for architectural work.

Baeli's priciest purchase, she calculates, were the windows at £30,000, while one of the cheapest measures was making the whole house airtight, which cost £5,000.

She says, like most people, she could not pay for everything at once and so decided to carry out the work in stages over ten years to spread the cost.

Although the house does prevent heat entering the home, it does need cooler air to start with.

As well as closing the windows and curtains during the day, Baeli says you need to ensure that "the sun doesn't hit the glass and create the glasshouse effect - to stop your home from overheating".

Outside in her garden she shows us dust sheets which have been hung up to cover the windows.

But if outdoor temperatures do not fall at night, as happened once during the June heatwave this summer, Baeli's house can remain hot. On that June evening, the nighttime temperatures was 27C so the house temperature remained at 27C, the highest Baeli has ever recorded in her home.

If such tropical nights occur again in the future, she says she might need to use air conditioning for a limited time to cool the house and then the Passivhaus measures can maintain that temperature.

How the UK's extreme heat is shifting the conversation about air-con

Including Passivhaus measures in a building's initial design is much cheaper than trying to add them retrospectively.

According to the Passivhaus Trust, the additional construction cost associated with building to the standard range from 2% extra for flats up to 5% for a semi-detached house.

In March, the Future Homes Standard will come into force which will set higher building and energy performance requirements for new homes in England - taking the regulations closer to the Passivhaus standards.

In Scotland, consultations for a new building regulations "to deliver an equivalent to the Passivhaus standard" are ongoing, and the new guidelines could be published later next year.

Meanwhile, one of the country's largest housebuilders, Barratt Redrow is building a block of affordable and private flats in west London to the standard - complete with heat pumps to heat and cool the properties.

Oliver Novakovic, the company's technical and innovation director, explains that even though it will cost more to apply the standard, the 900-apartment Bollo Lane development is an experiment to "future-proof" the company and stay ahead of "continually increasing" regulations.

Around 1% of all new homes in the country are now built to the voluntary standard, and the Passivhaus Trust estimates this could grow to 10% in the next decade. But building these types of new homes can be challenging. In April, City of York Council struggled to attract interest from construction firms to build 315 homes to the standard due to market conditions and the complexity of building to such specifications.

Even if new Passivhaus homes can be constructed, it is estimated that 80% of the UK housing stock in 2050 already exists today, so millions of homes will have to be retrofitted to cope with rising temperatures.

There is a government support system to help those in low-income households install insulation and other measures, but after reports of botched work it will close later this year. The date when the replacement scheme will begin has not been announced.

Jay Morton, incoming President Elect of the Royal Institute of British Architects, told BBC Radio 4's Rare Earth programme that cost can be a barrier for many homeowners, but that even implementing half these measures can make a significant difference.

"You won't necessarily be able to insulate every single wall," Morton says, "but by even doing the 50% best is actually massive in terms of energy bills."

For those in homes which are not built to the Passivhaus standard, Baeli offers one simple piece of advice - shade your windows.

"It doesn't need to be sophisticated," she says, "whatever you can do, just absolutely shade your windows and you will definitely feel the difference in the summer months."

The UK's summers are getting hotter - but how prepared are we?

‘It’s like an oven’: Life in Britain’s hottest areas

articles.title: How a new era of heatwaves could shake up the school calendar
articles.summary: Teachers warn it could be increasingly difficult for classrooms to function during the hottest months.
articles.body:
Over the past two weeks, the sound of children has returned to Scotland's school playgrounds. Their summer breaks began in late June or early July and ended in mid-August.

It's an academic year replicated in other European countries too.

In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, however, children will not return until early September. Their holidays are a similar length to Scotland's but England and Wales schools did not break up until late July, something that meant pupils were in school during the peak of the early summer heat.

Or at least they were meant to be in school. While it was 30C or more outside, inside many classrooms it felt far hotter. With no air conditioning and limited ventilation, the heat became stifling and more than 1,000 schools across the UK either closed or sent pupils home early before the hottest part of the afternoon. Conditions were particularly challenging for GCSE and A‑level students sitting exams during extreme heat.

Baroness Brown, chair of the UK's Climate Change Adaptation committee, has warned that "we know high temperatures can significantly impair concentration and performance" of children in schools.

Back in February 2026, Ofsted's chief inspector Sir Martyn Oliver said the timing of the school holidays should be reconsidered: "It's pretty hot usually in May, June and July, just at the point you're asking children to sit down and take an exam… so I think there is a need to have a good old look at it [the school year]."

The recent hot weather has seen some parents join his call. Andrea Bigger, a parent in London, is "absolutely aware of the dangers" of extreme heat in classrooms. She says her daughter has previously suffered from heat exhaustion and was hospitalised after overheating at her primary school. She is "really concerned that the UK is not ready or prepared for this".

And this summer was not a one off. BBC analysis of temperature data shows a clear shift. In the 1960s, the first 30C day was occurring on average on 13 July. In the 2020s that figure has been 19 June.

So, is it going to be increasingly difficult for schools to operate in the summer months? And is moving the school summer holidays the solution to ensuring pupils are able to be taught for as much of the year as possible?

This summer is likely to become the hottest on record, according to the Met Office. Multiple temperature records have been broken with five widespread heatwaves and four consecutive months where the temperature has exceeded 35C. This has never happened before.

June saw one of the UK's most intense heatwaves, with up to seven consecutive days where temperatures were well above the official heatwave thresholds of 25-28C - just as the exam period was in full swing. Temperature records were broken too: 38C was recorded in Lingwood, Norfolk on 26 June, the hottest June day ever measured in the UK.

The Met Office issued a red extreme heat warning at the end of June, while the UK Health Security Agency has issued multiple amber warnings over the last few months. The heat then continued into July, with heatwave conditions felt widely for most of the month.

Schools struggled to cope, with some closed declaring "heat days" as temperatures in classrooms became too high for children to concentrate. These kinds of disruptions, or heat days, could become more likely as human-induced climate change brings hotter summers and more frequent heatwaves.

Summer heat is arriving earlier. Will Lang, chief meteorologist at the Met Office, says the "de facto 'hot season' in the UK is lengthening, with increasing prevalence of hot weather - including heatwaves – in May and September in addition to the standard meteorological summer of June, July and August".

It's one sign of a warming climate reshaping the pattern and timing of UK summers.

According to a study conducted by the Met Office and University College London, students could lose an estimated 8.2 days of learning a year on average due to extreme heat, if average global average temperatures rise to more than 2C above pre-industiral levels - as many scientists believe will happen on current trajectories.

In the meantime, teachers are left to deal with the consequences.

Steve Chalke, founder of Oasis Academy, which runs more than 50 schools across England, says the heatwaves were a "real inhibitor" to teaching. One of the most difficult challenges came when the Met Office issued the red extreme heat warning at the end of June, suggesting potential "danger to life".

He says headteachers were forced into difficult decisions. "What do you do as a headteacher? How can they run a school safely if the national weather service is warning to travel only if essential and make every effort to stay cool. What if a student or member of staff collapses due to the heat and you're accountable for why you opened the school and didn't take your duty of care seriously?"

And with Met Office predictions of more extreme weather, higher summer temperatures, and more frequent, prolonged heatwaves, these types of questions are likely to only become more prevalent.

Rebecca Martin is concerned about her son taking GCSE exams in a few years' time in potentially increasingly hot weather. She thinks there needs to be "some serious considerations to the school year to reflect the changing climate or better investment in schools to give them air conditioning".

And there is growing evidence to support her worries. The recent Well-Adapted UK report from the Climate Change Committee suggested that taking an exam on a 32C day leads to around a 10% lower likelihood of passing, compared to sitting the same exam at 22C.

Baroness Brown told the BBC that "as heatwaves become more frequent and intense, it is unacceptable that children are expected to sit high-stakes exams in halls that were not designed for these conditions".

Many of us are familiar with a "snow day" in the winter, when snow can make it very difficult for staff and students to get into school. While there is no legal minimum temperature, the National Education Union says classrooms should be kept above 18C. Heat days are a newer concept - and there are no specified maximum temperatures for a classroom.

A 2024 study published in the journal Climate Risk Management suggested that any temperature above 24C can compromise learning. It also found a decline in student performance ranging from 2% to 12% for each degree increase in classroom temperature.

Setting a temperature benchmark of 26C as the upper "comfortable limit" in a classroom, the authors of the study went on to suggest that the average school currently reaches this limit 59 days of the year in England. That would increase to 71 days with 2C of warming.

In "at-risk" schools where there is no suitable ventilation or where newer buildings have lower ceilings, there would be 75 days where the "comfortable 26C classroom temperature would be breached".

In hotter European countries such as France and Spain, local authorities have extreme heat guidelines that trigger timetable changes or school closures when conditions become too hot. It's a model some argue the UK may need to consider as the UK summer continues to change.

While extreme heat or heatwaves can still occur in May and June - or indeed in late August or early September, by which time it's proposed pupils would have returned to class - breaking up for summer at the end of June could reduce the amount of disruption schools face from the hottest conditions heading into the peak of summer.

And while this August has also been hot and dry, some parents argue that an earlier break would be better aligned with the UK's typically warmer and drier mid-summer weather. Rebecca Martin says she'd like to be able to "make the most of the more guaranteed summer-like weather in July" planning to spend more time outdoors in a UK staycation rather than going abroad to parts of Europe where the "heat is getting even more extreme and unpleasant".

Europe is the fastest-warming continent, with temperatures rising at around twice the global average. Like the UK, European heatwaves are becoming hotter, more frequent and longer.

Staycations in the UK could become even more popular. According to 2024 research by Mintel, more than half of UK holidaymakers say they are likely to choose to holiday at home rather than abroad for climate-related reasons. Meanwhile, some 28% say higher UK temperatures are encouraging them to take domestic holidays.

What remains to be seen is how any changes to the school summer holiday could affect the price tag. Aligning the holiday period more closely with Scotland and other countries means there could be more demand in late June and July, potentially pushing the traditional price peak earlier in the year.

Other changing holiday habits - such as avoiding the peak of the summer heat and extreme temperatures in southern Europe - will also play a role.

In a recent national survey by InsureandGo, more than seven in 10 UK holidaymakers thought some European countries like Spain, Greece or Turkey would be too hot to visit in the summer months by the end of the decade.

As travel journalist Simon Calder has said: "A significant shift in holiday habits could push up the cost of a domestic holiday.

"If more people decide to stay in the UK, and others come to Britain because it is more climatically appealing, the rise in demand would trigger price increases. But there are always locations where you can get reasonable deals."

In England, term dates are determined by school employers - for maintained state schools, that's their local authority. Other schools, including academies, free schools, foundation schools and voluntary-aided schools, can set their own term dates.

However, any changes to the school holiday or academic year would likely require national‑level discussion and leadership, rather than decisions made by individual schools.

Steve Chalke of Oasis Academy suggested there needs to be a national plan with clear guidance for schools facing increasingly hot conditions in our warming climate.

"We're all accustomed to 'snow days' but we now need to properly think and prepare for 'heat days' too," he says. And "without doubt we need to rethink the school year".

For some parents, though, the answer isn't about changing the school holidays but making the school buildings more climate-resilient for the future.

A split in the spectrum? The ongoing battle to define autism

The dangers of politicians being 'too online' - or not online enough

Young adults are taking prescription drugs instead of alcohol - and it's dividing experts

Gemma Beake, a parent of two boys at a school in Bristol, suggests that if schools can be made cooler and have investment with air conditioning, they will be "safer places than a lot of homes and flats where we have the same problem of overheating".

British summers will always be variable, and no two years will be exactly alike. But the direction of travel is becoming clearer. Hot weather is arriving earlier, lasting longer and increasingly testing our school buildings that were designed and built in a past climate.

While headteachers can implement changes to uniform - as many did this year - so that PE kit could be worn instead of traditional uniform, for many it's the buildings that need adapting to the changing climate of today and especially the future.

But either upgrading infrastructure to climate resiliant schools or modifying the academic year would need institutional change with the possibility of a lot of investment. And both would take many years to implement.

For parents, teachers and school leaders however, changes are needed as soon as possible. As Steve Chalke puts it: "We need the government to come up with a short-term plan for the next few years."

This may simply mean better guidance during "heat days" and on when it is appropriate to shut schools, as with "snow days". Or just being more flexible - allowing schools to open earlier and finish earlier in the day to avoid a peak in temperatures.

paragraphs: Over the past two weeks, the sound of children has returned to Scotland's school playgrounds. Their summer breaks began in late June or early July and ended in mid-August.
It's an academic year replicated in other European countries too.

In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, however, children will not return until early September. Their holidays are a similar length to Scotland's but England and Wales schools did not break up until late July, something that meant pupils were in school during the peak of the early summer heat.

Or at least they were meant to be in school. While it was 30C or more outside, inside many classrooms it felt far hotter. With no air conditioning and limited ventilation, the heat became stifling and more than 1,000 schools across the UK either closed or sent pupils home early before the hottest part of the afternoon. Conditions were particularly challenging for GCSE and A‑level students sitting exams during extreme heat.
Baroness Brown, chair of the UK's Climate Change Adaptation committee, has warned that "we know high temperatures can significantly impair concentration and performance" of children in schools.

Back in February 2026, Ofsted's chief inspector Sir Martyn Oliver said the timing of the school holidays should be reconsidered: "It's pretty hot usually in May, June and July, just at the point you're asking children to sit down and take an exam… so I think there is a need to have a good old look at it [the school year]."

The recent hot weather has seen some parents join his call. Andrea Bigger, a parent in London, is "absolutely aware of the dangers" of extreme heat in classrooms. She says her daughter has previously suffered from heat exhaustion and was hospitalised after overheating at her primary school. She is "really concerned that the UK is not ready or prepared for this".

And this summer was not a one off. BBC analysis of temperature data shows a clear shift. In the 1960s, the first 30C day was occurring on average on 13 July. In the 2020s that figure has been 19 June.

So, is it going to be increasingly difficult for schools to operate in the summer months? And is moving the school summer holidays the solution to ensuring pupils are able to be taught for as much of the year as possible?

This summer is likely to become the hottest on record, according to the Met Office. Multiple temperature records have been broken with five widespread heatwaves and four consecutive months where the temperature has exceeded 35C. This has never happened before.

June saw one of the UK's most intense heatwaves, with up to seven consecutive days where temperatures were well above the official heatwave thresholds of 25-28C - just as the exam period was in full swing. Temperature records were broken too: 38C was recorded in Lingwood, Norfolk on 26 June, the hottest June day ever measured in the UK.

The Met Office issued a red extreme heat warning at the end of June, while the UK Health Security Agency has issued multiple amber warnings over the last few months. The heat then continued into July, with heatwave conditions felt widely for most of the month.

Schools struggled to cope, with some closed declaring "heat days" as temperatures in classrooms became too high for children to concentrate. These kinds of disruptions, or heat days, could become more likely as human-induced climate change brings hotter summers and more frequent heatwaves.

Summer heat is arriving earlier. Will Lang, chief meteorologist at the Met Office, says the "de facto 'hot season' in the UK is lengthening, with increasing prevalence of hot weather - including heatwaves – in May and September in addition to the standard meteorological summer of June, July and August".
It's one sign of a warming climate reshaping the pattern and timing of UK summers.

According to a study conducted by the Met Office and University College London, students could lose an estimated 8.2 days of learning a year on average due to extreme heat, if average global average temperatures rise to more than 2C above pre-industiral levels - as many scientists believe will happen on current trajectories.
In the meantime, teachers are left to deal with the consequences.

Steve Chalke, founder of Oasis Academy, which runs more than 50 schools across England, says the heatwaves were a "real inhibitor" to teaching. One of the most difficult challenges came when the Met Office issued the red extreme heat warning at the end of June, suggesting potential "danger to life".

He says headteachers were forced into difficult decisions. "What do you do as a headteacher? How can they run a school safely if the national weather service is warning to travel only if essential and make every effort to stay cool. What if a student or member of staff collapses due to the heat and you're accountable for why you opened the school and didn't take your duty of care seriously?"
And with Met Office predictions of more extreme weather, higher summer temperatures, and more frequent, prolonged heatwaves, these types of questions are likely to only become more prevalent.

Rebecca Martin is concerned about her son taking GCSE exams in a few years' time in potentially increasingly hot weather. She thinks there needs to be "some serious considerations to the school year to reflect the changing climate or better investment in schools to give them air conditioning".

And there is growing evidence to support her worries. The recent Well-Adapted UK report from the Climate Change Committee suggested that taking an exam on a 32C day leads to around a 10% lower likelihood of passing, compared to sitting the same exam at 22C.

Baroness Brown told the BBC that "as heatwaves become more frequent and intense, it is unacceptable that children are expected to sit high-stakes exams in halls that were not designed for these conditions".

Many of us are familiar with a "snow day" in the winter, when snow can make it very difficult for staff and students to get into school. While there is no legal minimum temperature, the National Education Union says classrooms should be kept above 18C. Heat days are a newer concept - and there are no specified maximum temperatures for a classroom.

A 2024 study published in the journal Climate Risk Management suggested that any temperature above 24C can compromise learning. It also found a decline in student performance ranging from 2% to 12% for each degree increase in classroom temperature.

Setting a temperature benchmark of 26C as the upper "comfortable limit" in a classroom, the authors of the study went on to suggest that the average school currently reaches this limit 59 days of the year in England. That would increase to 71 days with 2C of warming.
In "at-risk" schools where there is no suitable ventilation or where newer buildings have lower ceilings, there would be 75 days where the "comfortable 26C classroom temperature would be breached".

In hotter European countries such as France and Spain, local authorities have extreme heat guidelines that trigger timetable changes or school closures when conditions become too hot. It's a model some argue the UK may need to consider as the UK summer continues to change.

While extreme heat or heatwaves can still occur in May and June - or indeed in late August or early September, by which time it's proposed pupils would have returned to class - breaking up for summer at the end of June could reduce the amount of disruption schools face from the hottest conditions heading into the peak of summer.

And while this August has also been hot and dry, some parents argue that an earlier break would be better aligned with the UK's typically warmer and drier mid-summer weather. Rebecca Martin says she'd like to be able to "make the most of the more guaranteed summer-like weather in July" planning to spend more time outdoors in a UK staycation rather than going abroad to parts of Europe where the "heat is getting even more extreme and unpleasant".
Europe is the fastest-warming continent, with temperatures rising at around twice the global average. Like the UK, European heatwaves are becoming hotter, more frequent and longer.

Staycations in the UK could become even more popular. According to 2024 research by Mintel, more than half of UK holidaymakers say they are likely to choose to holiday at home rather than abroad for climate-related reasons. Meanwhile, some 28% say higher UK temperatures are encouraging them to take domestic holidays.

What remains to be seen is how any changes to the school summer holiday could affect the price tag. Aligning the holiday period more closely with Scotland and other countries means there could be more demand in late June and July, potentially pushing the traditional price peak earlier in the year.
Other changing holiday habits - such as avoiding the peak of the summer heat and extreme temperatures in southern Europe - will also play a role.

In a recent national survey by InsureandGo, more than seven in 10 UK holidaymakers thought some European countries like Spain, Greece or Turkey would be too hot to visit in the summer months by the end of the decade.
As travel journalist Simon Calder has said: "A significant shift in holiday habits could push up the cost of a domestic holiday.

"If more people decide to stay in the UK, and others come to Britain because it is more climatically appealing, the rise in demand would trigger price increases. But there are always locations where you can get reasonable deals."

In England, term dates are determined by school employers - for maintained state schools, that's their local authority. Other schools, including academies, free schools, foundation schools and voluntary-aided schools, can set their own term dates.
However, any changes to the school holiday or academic year would likely require national‑level discussion and leadership, rather than decisions made by individual schools.
Steve Chalke of Oasis Academy suggested there needs to be a national plan with clear guidance for schools facing increasingly hot conditions in our warming climate.
"We're all accustomed to 'snow days' but we now need to properly think and prepare for 'heat days' too," he says. And "without doubt we need to rethink the school year".
For some parents, though, the answer isn't about changing the school holidays but making the school buildings more climate-resilient for the future.

The dangers of politicians being 'too online' - or not online enough
Young adults are taking prescription drugs instead of alcohol - and it's dividing experts

Gemma Beake, a parent of two boys at a school in Bristol, suggests that if schools can be made cooler and have investment with air conditioning, they will be "safer places than a lot of homes and flats where we have the same problem of overheating".

British summers will always be variable, and no two years will be exactly alike. But the direction of travel is becoming clearer. Hot weather is arriving earlier, lasting longer and increasingly testing our school buildings that were designed and built in a past climate.

While headteachers can implement changes to uniform - as many did this year - so that PE kit could be worn instead of traditional uniform, for many it's the buildings that need adapting to the changing climate of today and especially the future.

But either upgrading infrastructure to climate resiliant schools or modifying the academic year would need institutional change with the possibility of a lot of investment. And both would take many years to implement.
For parents, teachers and school leaders however, changes are needed as soon as possible. As Steve Chalke puts it: "We need the government to come up with a short-term plan for the next few years."

This may simply mean better guidance during "heat days" and on when it is appropriate to shut schools, as with "snow days". Or just being more flexible - allowing schools to open earlier and finish earlier in the day to avoid a peak in temperatures.

articles.title: Saltash man completes 2,800 mile scoot across Australia
articles.summary: Bob Brown from Saltash has ridden a non-electric scooter from Perth to Sydney.
articles.body:
A man has completed a challenge to cross the width of Australia on a non-electric kick scooter.

Bob Brown from Saltash, Cornwall started his journey in July and travelled about 2,800 miles (4506km) from Perth to Sydney, where he finished his trip on Monday.

He said he hoped to break two Guinness World Records - to become the fastest person to cross the country on a kick scooter, while also being the first to travel the route by three different methods, running, cycling, and scootering.

Brown said "after a lifetime packed with adventure, at 57-years-old I wanted another epic adventure before I got too old".

Brown's is no stranger to the country and hoped to raise £5,000 for three charities - MacMillan Cancer Support, St Luke's Hospice and Children's Hospice South West.

In 2001 be became the first Briton to run across the country covering 3,000 miles (4828.032km) in 60 days, before in 2003 he cycled the route becoming the first person to have both run and cycled across Australia.

"I wanted to raise awareness of the need for youngsters to get off their screens and devices and to seek out adventure", he said.

He said he got injured while completing the challenge.

"On day five my wing mirror got clipped by a passing vehicle and I skidded onto the hard shoulder" but was "relatively unscathed".

"Also on the last day, with just 20km to go, I had a serious fall when my handlebars broke going down a steep hill", he added.

Despite the complications, Brown completed the challenge in 31 days, four hours and 10 minutes.

He said he had submitted his documentation to Guinness but had to wait to see if the organisation would officially recognise his achievements.

articles.title: Pakistan army chief Asim Munir to visit Iran amid push to revive stalled US talks
articles.summary: Middle East News: Pakistan Army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir will travel to Tehran on Monday for talks with Iranian leaders as Islamabad seeks to revive stalled effor.
articles.body: Pakistan Army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir will travel to Tehran on Monday for talks with Iranian leaders as Islamabad seeks to revive stalled efforts to bring the United States and Iran back to the negotiating table.Iran's foreign ministry announced the visit on Sunday, saying Munir will discuss bilateral ties and regional issues during his stay. He will be accompanied by a delegation that is expected to hold high-level discussions with the Iranian leadership.The visit comes as Pakistan steps up efforts to mediate between Washington and Tehran after an agreement intended to create a 60-day window for high-level peace talks fell apart last month.Pakistan's mediation effortsPakistan had signed the interim peace agreement as a guarantor. However, the arrangement broke down as tensions in West Asia intensified and the US and Iran resumed military strikes.Pakistan has since been trying to restart the diplomatic process. Interior minister Mohsin Naqvi travelled to Tehran earlier this month, where he met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said on Sunday that Munir's visit would focus on strengthening cooperation between the two countries and supporting efforts to promote peace and security in the region.Pakistan has not yet officially commented on the army chief's planned visit.Why the talks broke downThe stalled process followed a memorandum of understanding signed by the US and Iran in June. The agreement was intended to provide a 60-day period for high-level negotiations aimed at restoring peace in West Asia.However, the talks collapsed after tensions between Washington and Tehran escalated again in mid-July. Pakistan's subsequent attempts to bring the two sides back to negotiations have so far failed to produce a breakthrough.A major obstacle is the Strait of Hormuz, a key global shipping route that has been disrupted by the conflict. The war began on February 28 after the US and Israel launched joint attacks on Iran, prompting retaliatory strikes from Tehran. Under normal circumstances, around one-fifth of the world's energy supplies passes through the Gulf chokepoint.Iran warns against economic pressureIranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Sunday defended the June agreement as the best way for Tehran to move beyond what he described as a situation of âneither war nor peaceâ.At the same time, Mohsen Rezaei, the hard-line new head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, warned neighbouring countries against joining a fresh US effort to put pressure on Iran's economy.US President Donald Trump had warned on August 20 that Washington would launch what he called the âmost crushing economic operationâ against Iran if Tehran failed to reach a deal.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Leah Stewart: Australian shark attack victim grateful for 'second chance at life'
articles.summary: Leah Stewart was mauled by a shark in June, suffering multiple bites to her arms and legs.
articles.body:
An Australian woman bitten by a shark at a popular Sydney beach earlier this year says she has been given a "second chance at life" and will be making the most of it.

Leah Stewart, 34, was mauled by a shark during a morning swim at Coogee Beach in June, suffering multiple bites to her arms and legs, amid a spate of attacks in Australia.

The mother-of-one was placed in an induced coma and had several surgeries, including having one of her arms amputated.

In an online post on Monday, she thanked her supporters who have raised more than AU$550,000 (US$394,000; £289,000) for her, saying her recovery has been "incredibly difficult" but she is making "remarkable" progress.

"After what has been an incredibly difficult few months, I'm so happy that I've progressed enough to build some independence, and I can finally see some light after all of this," Stewart wrote, in her first comments since the attack.

"I want you to know that I feel like I've been given a second chance at life, and I'm not going to waste it."

Stewart said she had been "overwhelmed" by the support from family, friends and "even strangers", adding that the "you've inspired me to get better, not bitter".

An online fundraiser for her would now be closed, she wrote, with the money raised giving her the chance to recover at home as well as "options for further medical treatment down the road".

"I still have a long way to go, but my recovery has been remarkable, and a huge part of that is because of the absolute army of love, support, prayers and encouragement surrounding my family and I from all over the world."

In an interview with Nine Network's 60 Minutes, due to be aired this weekend, Stewart described seeing the shark's "horrific" face.

"I'll never forget its face - it was a monster," she says.

"It was holding onto my leg and I just thought of (my daughter) August, and I thought, 'she's not going to have a mum. She's gonna grow up without a mum'."

Fighting back tears, she goes on: "I couldn't handle that, I didn't want her to not have a mum. I just thought, I've got to fight it, do everything I can to be here."

There have been a spate of shark attacks in Australia this year, with four attacks over a two-day period in January, including one on a 12-year-old boy who later died from his injuries.

In May, a man was killed by a shark in Queensland while spearfishing and in Western Australia, a father-of-two died after he was attacked by a 4m (13ft) shark.

articles.title: Ex-cricket captains call on Pakistan to ensure 'proper medical care' for Imran Khan
articles.summary: The former skippers say it is "basic decency" for Pakistan to comply with a court-ordered medical assessment.
articles.body:
A group of former cricket captains, including Indian batting legend Sunil Gavaskar and one of England's longest-serving skippers Sir Alastair Cook, have called on Pakistan to ensure its ex-PM Imran Khan be given proper care while in custody.

The cricketer-turned-politician has been in jail since 2023 on corruption charges which he denies.

In a letter to Pakistan's current leader Shehbaz Sharif, the 21 former skippers aired concern that Khan, 73, was allowed "only a few hours" at a hospital last week where he was examined by a state-appointed team.

Khan's party has also filed a contempt petition against the government for not giving him access to his own doctors, as ordered by the top court.

The former cricket captains laid out three demands in their letter, the first of which is that Khan be assessed by a medical board directed by Pakistan's Supreme Court – which would include his personal physicians – particularly on the reported loss of vision in his right eye.

They also urged authorities to allow weekly visits by Khan's family, as ordered by the court, "without interruptions or administrative delays".

Finally, they asked that any treatment recommended by the medical board be "provided without delay".

"Imran Khan is 73 years old and has now spent more than three years in custody," read the letter initiated by former Australian captain Greg Chappell.

"Whatever the legal and political arguments surrounding his case, the basic decency of ensuring a court-ordered medical process is actually completed is not, in our view, a controversial request."

Among the other signatories were England's Michael Atherton, Michael Brearley, Nasser Hussain, Andrew Strauss and David Gower, India's Kapil Dev and Dilip Vengsarkar, and Australia's Belinda Clark, Adam Gilchrist, Steve Waugh and Kim Hughes.

Fourteen of the former skippers had also supported an earlier appeal for "humane treatment and proper medical care" for Khan which was submitted in February.

Khan's lawyer claimed at the time that his client had 15% vision left in his right eye after prison authorities failed to take action.

The signatories of both letters had described themselves as "former colleagues and rivals who share a bond forged on the cricket field", adding that the bond "transcends the borders and disputes that too often divide countries".

Khan, who previously captained the Pakistan national cricket team, served as Pakistan's prime minister from 2018 to 2022.

He was imprisoned in August 2023 and has faced charges in more than 100 cases, ranging from leaking state secrets to selling state gifts, all of which he and his party Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf say are politically motivated.

His jailing sparked large-scale protests by supporters, which were met with a crackdown by authorities.

Pakistan's Supreme Court had on Tuesday directed the government to transfer Khan to a private hospital to be examined by physicians.

He was instead seen by doctors at a government-run hospital in Islamabad, who deemed him "medically fit", before he was moved back to prison.

articles.title: Keeping London's canal boats afloat during summer drought
articles.summary: Locks on the Grand Union canal in are closed at night in hopes of managing water levels downstream.
articles.body:
Drought conditions in the capital mean that London's waterways are being more actively managed to maintain water levels.

In west London on the Grand Union Canal, the gates of six locks known as the Hanwell Flight have been locked up at night with their paddles shut to prevent misuse that impacts the canal downstream.

Colin Beesley, waterway operative at Canal and River Trust, described the situation as "unprecedented", adding: "It's been one of the driest summers we've ever seen and of course there's been virtually no rain.

"Because this drought has been extending for so long, we've made the decision to lock this flight of locks overnight."

Additionally, all of the lock gates have been "ashed up", a traditional method of sealing gaps between planks in lock gates with coal dust to hold water in.

The action on the Hanwell Flight has helped maintain water levels at the "Long Pound", a 27 mile (43.4km) lock-free stretch which encompasses the Grand Union Main Line, Paddington Arm and Regent's Canal all the way to Camden.

In east London, closures are also helping to manage the water levels.

Charlotte Wood, head of operations at the Canal and River Trust, explained that they have closed the Hertford Union Canal, a 1.2 mile (2km) long stretch of water that acts as a short-cut from the Regent's Canal to the River Lee, avoiding the River Thames.

Wood said the "non-critical" route near Victoria Park was closed so that water coming in from west London from the Hanwell Flight area and beyond went into central London.

"We're keeping the Regent's Canal open for as long as possible for our boats to move and to keep afloat," she added.

In Hanwell, boats are still allowed to travel through the canal during the day, but for boaters like Paul Findlay, the drought has made things much more challenging.

Nicholas Jones, area operations manager at the Canal and River Trust, said they were using an app to monitor water levels, and were also keeping a close eye on the weather, adding that he was "deeply desperate" for rain to return to the capital.

"We get hopeful whenever it starts to speckle slightly, but it generally never arrives," he said.

This stretch of the Grand Union Canal has been open since 1794 - all the locks need now is more water to fill them.

articles.title: UK's rarest bird of prey rears new chicks in secret location
articles.summary: The Montagu Harrier successfully nested for the second year running in the same secret location.
articles.body:
The UK's rarest bird of prey has successfully nested for the second year running in the same secret location, the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB) has reported.

A male Montagu's harrier, known as "AU" by conservationists, bred with two different females, rearing six chicks across two nests on English farmland.

Montagu's harriers were put on a "red list" of birds most at risk in the UK in 2021. Numbers have declined from a high of nine successful nests in 2011, to no evidence of successful breeding between 2020 and 2024.

An RSPB spokesperson said: "We are doing our absolute utmost to save this iconic species in the UK and are delighted with six flying juveniles this year."

Four chicks hatched in the same secret location last year.

The charity said careful monitoring, in partnership with the farmers on whose land the birds nested, meant the nests were protected by fences to exclude ground predators such as foxes.

The single male Montagu's harrier has also been working very hard to keep his two nests of hungry chicks fed.

The BBC was given exclusive access to the nest and was able to witness some of the spectacular feeding behaviour of the raptors: the male drops prey in mid-air and the female rolls upside down to catch it in her talons.

These slender, long-winged raptors make an epic annual migration to Africa in winter and return to Europe to nest over summer, often setting up home in agricultural fields.

But little is known about the behaviour of juvenile harriers once they leave the nest. This year, for the first time, the RSPB has fitted two of the chicks with satellite tags in the hope of providing the birds with better protection.

"It will allow us for the first time ever to work out where they're going, what migration route, how long they'll spend there, and will they come back to the UK in the first year or the second year," said Mark Thomas, head of investigations at the RSPB.

"All of that information is the bit that's missing from the jigsaw."

It is also hoped the tagging can better protect the rare birds from having their nests, on the ground, hidden among crops, inadvertently destroyed.

"This is a species right on the brink, and climate change is not helping that. The harvest here, for example, this year, was like a month earlier than in previous years. So it almost puts any Montagu's harrier nest at the peril of inadvertently being destroyed by farm machinery," said Thomas.

Conservationists have urged birders to look out for the youngsters, and report any sightings by emailing the RSPB's Montagu's hotline at montys@rspb.org.uk.

articles.title: UK missiles offer may help Ukraine - but they are not what Zelensky needs most
articles.summary: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham is handing over blueprints so Kyiv can build its own long-range missiles.
articles.body:
The UK is set to hand over blueprints for its British-French designed Storm Shadow cruise missiles to Ukraine – following a similar move from France – allowing Ukraine to produce the weapon domestically.

The move sends an important signal, showing that some Western nations are willing to share their expertise and know how to help Ukraine defend itself.

But, on its own, this won't dramatically alter the course of the war.

Scalp and Storm Shadow missiles have already been provided to Kyiv by both Britain and France. They've already been used to hit military targets inside Russia.

Burnham to hand long-range missile blueprints to Zelensky as he visits Kyiv

The weapons are not new – they were developed in the 1990s - and they are expensive – at around £1m a piece.

They also rely on complex global supply chains and have been built in peacetime at relatively low rates – in the hundreds, not the thousands.

Even with the blueprints, Ukraine may find it hard to source components. It could take months, possibly years to make the cruise missile themselves.

Copying Western weapons production in peacetime is, in fact, no way to win a war. Even Nato nations now realise that.

Britain and many of its allies have tended to produce small quantities of highly advanced, expensive missiles which would quickly run out in any protracted conflict.

In 2021, the former head of the US Army in Europe, Gen Ben Hodges, said that in a Nato wargame the UK military ran out of key weapons within a matter of days.

Proof of the recent change in mindset is the UK military is no longer buying Storm Shadow missiles for itself.

Instead, under Project Brakestop, it is developing its own long-range cruise missiles, free of foreign components, and less than half the price of a Storm Shadow.

Project Brakestop is also being done at break-neck speed. The UK hopes to have a new cruise missile ready by the end of the year. It is promising to supply the new weapon to Ukraine.

It is Ukraine which has shown the world how to produce relatively cheap, mass produced weapons, necessary for a long, protracted conflict.

Douglas Barrie, Senior Fellow for Military Aerospace at the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) told the BBC: "The decision to share UK classified information on the MBDA SCALP missiles with Ukraine, as France and Ukraine work toward local assembly lines in Ukraine, is notable. Any impact, however, will in part depend on how quickly Ukrainian assembled SCALP cruise missiles can be introduced into service.

"Given that Ukraine has already operated both Storm Shadow and SCALP, familiarity with the missile may help speed the overall process, but this will also be dependent on the extent and pace at which local assembly can be established."

At the start of the war its armed forces relied on old Cold War-era Soviet weaponry.

A slow supply of Western weapons helped it adapt. But now Ukraine produces 70% of its own weapons.

Key has been its rapid development of drone technology – from small First Person View (FPV) one-way attack drones for the front line, to larger long-range drones capable of striking deep into Russian territory, further than Storm Shadows can strike.

Kyiv is on track to build 10 million drones by the end of this year. And they can do it cheaper than the West, by using mass-produced Chinese parts.

Nato allies' equivalent drones can be twice as expensive as they try to shun Chinese components.

However, there are still weapons that Ukraine needs and struggles to produce on its own. From fast fighter jets to the most urgent example, interceptors to take down Russian ballistic missiles

The most effective weapon to do that, by far, is the US-made Patriot interceptor. Ukraine has all but run out of them and Russian ballistic missiles now make it through Ukrainian air defences with ease.

America's war in Iran has meant they're in even shorter supply.

They're also expensive – at around £3m a missile – and production rates have been slow. The US is planning to double production rates from around 600 Patriot missiles per annum to 2,000, but that will take several years.

President Donald Trump signalled last month that he would be willing to share Patriot technology with Ukraine, but has since rowed back .

Even if he had given approval, it would have taken a while for Ukraine to make Patriots themselves - some estimate at least a year. Ukraine would also be relying on the same sophisticated components that are in high demand across the globe.

Ukraine has embarked on a programme to develop its own interceptor missiles with European support – known as Project Freya.

But there are huge technological challenges in building a high-speed missile to take down another missile travelling at thousands of miles per hour. It is expensive and often time consuming.

Ukraine's military and its weapons manufacturers have shown themselves to be fast learners.

One of its own companies, Fire Point, is developing its own ballistic missiles which it hopes will be ready to fire in anger next year.

But Russia has already ramped up its own ballistic missile production, to around 100 a month.

Developing sophisticated weapons is expensive and cannot be done quickly. Ukraine is short of both time and money.

So, the move to hand missile blueprints to Ukraine will be welcome, but it is not an immediate fix for Ukraine's most pressing problems, and it wwill not dramatically alter Kyiv's ability to strike Russia in new ways.

articles.title: Rumours swirled after a Vietnamese teen was run over - then came a stunning admission
articles.summary: Confirmation of the circumstances around Do Ngoc Phuong Thuy's death have only spurred more questions.
articles.body:
Until recently, there would have been little to distinguish Vietnam's so-called Justice Tree from the hundreds of others lining the streets of Hanoi. Then the bouquets started piling up.

It was here that former politician Nguyen Sy Cuong was driving his BMW in May last year when he veered into the opposite lane and smashed into a motorbike carrying a father and his teenage daughter.

The father, Do Viet Hung, suffered a broken leg but survived. The daughter, 18-year-old Do Ngoc Phuong Thuy, died in hospital 10 days after the collision, which severed her right leg.

Fifteen months later, her death and the silence surrounding it has become a lightning rod for discontent among Vietnam's youth.

In early August, a legion of anonymous social media users started publishing millions of posts with the hashtags #NguyenSyCuong and #BMW across Facebook, Instagram, Threads and X. The users identified themselves as Gen Z – and they demanded accountability.

Initial discussions circled around whether the former politician was in fact the one who had caused the accident, and why authorities had only released sparse information.

Some pointed to reports that the driver of the BMW had the initials NSC and was born in 1961, leading to speculation that he was a former member of parliament. Others claimed the incident had been swept under the rug due to the influence of powerful figures.

Many reported that their posts had been deleted by social media platforms at the request of the Vietnamese government – providing screenshots of notifications as evidence. These claims could not be independently verified.

Expressions of outrage and calls for a proper investigation grew in number, volume and force.

Meanwhile, masked flower bearers started to appear, gravitating towards the scene of the incident and laying vibrant bouquets at the base of what has now been dubbed the Justice Tree. Police quickly arrived to get rid of the flowers, prompting mourners to create a virtual equivalent of the tree online - where hundreds of thousands of people have since sent tributes and paid respects.

Pressurised by more than a year's worth of growing suspicion and a rush of online attention, the issue had become too big to ignore.

Then, last Monday, the government made an extraordinary admission.

State broadcaster Vietnam Television (VTV) televised an official statement from authorities, confirming what had happened on the day of the incident. Former National Assembly deputy Nguyen Sy Cuong was indeed driving his car down Nguyen Huy Tu Street on 30 May, 2025, when his vehicle suddenly swerved across the road and into an oncoming motorcycle.

VTV cited police and prosecution sources who said that because Nguyen Sy Cuong "sincerely confessed and actively and fully remedied the consequences of his actions", Do Ngoc Phuong Thuy's family had submitted a petition to exempt him from prosecution. The report did not specify what form this remedy took, but Nguyen Sy Cuong was cleared of all criminal liability.

While such a decision is lawful under Vietnam's legislation, lawyers have questioned whether the criminal proceedings were conducted in accordance with due process – or conducted at all. Social media users were quick to highlight his political connections and call for a more thorough investigation.

Such online pressure had yielded results in the past.

In March this year, a 66-year-old man driving under the influence of alcohol in Hanoi collided with seven other cars and three motorcycles in a chain-reaction crash that killed one woman and seriously injured two others.

In the wake of that incident, it emerged that the driver, Nguyen Van Sau, was a retired police colonel who had previously served as deputy director of a department under the Ministry of Public Security. Fearing that the driver was not being held culpable, the victim's family appealed for help. Social media users in turn amplified the issue, and after three months Nguyen Van Sau was charged with "violating regulations on participation in road traffic".

Who is To Lam, the ex-cop who wants to revamp Vietnam's success story?

British teen dies in reported Vietnam motorbike fall

Jailed Vietnamese tycoon's Birkin bags sell for more than $550K

Many now feel that a similar groundswell may be the only way to deliver justice for the teenager who died last year. But their efforts have been met with friction.

Do Viet Hung, the teenager's father, appeared in VTV's broadcast to thank internet users for their sympathy, but said the family was satisfied with the investigation's findings, and asked people to leave them alone. Notably, he also warned people "not to be drawn into the influence of reactionary elements".

Also appearing in the broadcast was a senior police official, who suggested that people were leveraging the incident to stoke dissent.

The Ministry of Public Security had "uncovered highly dangerous plots and intentions by hostile forces, reactionaries and bad actors to incite unrest and cause disorder", the official said.

"The ministry advises the public, especially young people, to remain fully alert and highly vigilant."

Similar rebukes have also started emerging on social media, with some claiming that conspiratorial forces were manipulating young people in Vietnam to stoke political discontent, manipulate public opinion online and rally people in real life ahead of the country's national holiday on 2 September.

Others have accused Gen Z Vietnamese of plotting a "colour revolution" – a term used to refer to mostly nonviolent protest movements that use specific colours or flowers as their symbol.

This is a familiar line of critique from Vietnamese authorities, who have previously labelled people's grievances or resentments as being untrue, unreasonable, or stemming from information fabricated by some "anti-government" or "reactionary" organisation.

Many in this case have said such accusations are baseless, insisting they are simply seeking justice for the victim of a fatal traffic accident. But the growing outrage has inevitably become a flashpoint amid broader, simmering grievances felt by Vietnam's youth.

Despite the Vietnamese government's tightening control over people's online freedom of expression – through measures ranging from intimidation and fines to criminal prosecution – public opinion in some corners has started to swerve against the Communist Party line.

On platforms such as Threads and Reddit, where anonymity is more normalised, many young people have expressed discontent towards various social issues: from the expansion of police power and land reclamation projects to exam cheating scandals and stricter regulation of online communication.

Such grievances echo those condemned by other Gen Z-led movements across the broader Asia region.

In countries like Bangladesh, India and Nepal, youth-led anti-government uprisings have over the past 12 months rallied immense support against the various pressure points of corruption, nepotism, economic inequality and democratic backsliding. Unofficially dubbed "the Asian Spring", the expanding influence of these movements has spread from Iran, Mongolia and the Maldives to the Philippines and Timor-Leste.

But protests in Vietnam have rarely, if ever, reached such fierce extremes. Vietnamese authorities have historically proven effective at detecting and stifling dissent before it boils over into action. Virtual places of mourning, anonymous social media posts, and online protests seem to be the most strident action many civilians here can afford to take.

Many are simply seeking justice for a teenager who was killed in a tragic accident, and accountability for a former lawmaker who appears to have been granted special clemency.

Yet even the mere suggestion that this incident could foment an uprising has provoked alarm – along with harsh reminders of the longstanding status quo in Vietnam's one-party state.

"Are these Gen Z kids planning a colour revolution using this accident?" reads one widely shared post. "Are they trying to emulate Bangladesh, India, and Nepal, and then create an Asian Spring? Remember, this is Vietnam! This is not Nepal, India, or Bangladesh!"

Virtual places of mourning, anonymous social media posts, and online protests seem to be the most strident action many civilians here can afford to take.
Many are simply seeking justice for a teenager who was killed in a tragic accident, and accountability for a former lawmaker who appears to have been granted special clemency.
Yet even the mere suggestion that this incident could foment an uprising has provoked alarm – along with harsh reminders of the longstanding status quo in Vietnam's one-party state.

"Are these Gen Z kids planning a colour revolution using this accident?" reads one widely shared post. "Are they trying to emulate Bangladesh, India, and Nepal, and then create an Asian Spring? Remember, this is Vietnam! This is not Nepal, India, or Bangladesh!"

Vietnam authorities have confirmed that former politician Nguyen Sy Cuong was driving the car that crashed into an 18-year-old and her father last year [Supplied: Government of Vietnam]

articles.title: Outrage in Nepal over rape and murder of three-year-old girl
articles.summary: There have been protests since the girl was found dead last week, three days after she went missing.
articles.body:
Activists and politicians in Nepal have urged the government to enact tougher laws as the alleged rape and murder of a three-year-old girl has caused outrage across the country.

Nepal has seen continued protests since the girl was found dead last week, three days after she went missing in Madhesh province.

Nine people have been arrested in connection with the case, a local police spokesman told the BBC.

The crime has triggered demands for reform. Police have also been accused of negligence in the initial stages of the investigation after footage of a teenage suspect was leaked onto social media.

After days of demonstrations in the city of Simara, the victim's family met government ministers, and secured a written agreement over the weekend.

The government has promised to review laws on serious offences, and create a memorial in honour of the child.

The incident has also opened a wider debate over how Nepal deals with young offenders, with some campaigners pushing for harsher punishments for minors convicted of rape or murder.

Prominent human rights activist Gauri Pradhan called the attack a "very painful incident and the government should punish anyone involved in such atrocious act. There should be some serious efforts for wider reforms".

However, he cautioned against calls for the introduction of the death penalty.

There has also been anger after a video showing a teenage suspect giving a statement about the suspected murder was uploaded to social media, sparking questions as to how footage of the individual under police custody was leaked.

"We have so far found one police personnel directly involved in the [leak] and have initiated action against him," chief district officer of Bara district, Dharmendra Kumar Mishra, told the BBC.

"If more officers are found, they will also be punished. We have zero tolerance against such practice."

More than 25,500 accusations of rape and sexual abuse were filed between July 2017 to July 2025, according to Nepalese Police.

Of these cases, more than 3,200 female victims were under the age of 10, the police say.

articles.title: Abbott tells judge Minnesota’s ICE officer extradition lawsuit ‘doomed to fail’
articles.summary: Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) asserted to a judge Monday that he’s not obligated to hand over an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer charged by Mi...
articles.body:
Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) asserted to a judge Monday that he's not obligated to hand over an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer charged by Minnesota authorities with shooting a Venezuelan man earlier this year during "Operation Metro Surge."

Minnesota is pushing in court to force the extradition of ICE officer Christian Castro, with a key hearing slated for Tuesday. The state insists Abbott has no discretion to avoid signing the warrant.

"In the end, Minnesota's zeal to see Mr. Castro prosecuted on its home turf cannot justify pretermitting Governor Abbott's ongoing deliberations pursuant to the Constitution and state statutes, which are designed to protect against abusive and baseless deprivations of individual liberty," Abbott's lawyers wrote in their formal written response to the court.

U.S. District Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr., an appointee of President Trump who oversees the case, will consider Minnesota's bid at a Tuesday afternoon hearing in his Brownsville, Texas, courtroom.

It has become a major legal clash between Abbott and Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz (D), who requested Castro's extradition as state authorities charged the ICE officer with four counts of second-degree assault and one count of falsely reporting a crime.

The officer stands accused of injuring a Venezuelan man in the leg by firing a gun at the front door of an occupied Minneapolis home on Jan. 14 amid an immigration enforcement surge in the Twin Cities. Castro had allegedly told investigators he opened fire in self-defense after being hit with a shovel and a broom, only for video footage to undercut the officer's claim.

Abbott has refused to sign a rendition warrant that would pave the way for the officer to return to Minnesota for trial.

In the new filing, the governor's lawyers raised doubts that Castro qualifies for the Constitution's extradition requirement. It demands a state return defendants facing criminal charges who "flee from Justice" when they are "found in another State." Abbott has suggested Castro didn't flee because ICE had ordered him to return to Texas.

"The ordinary meaning of a fugitive entails a volitional act of fleeing, not mere involuntary movement across state lines," his lawyers wrote.

Minnesota insists that Abbott's role is ministerial, and the state wants a judge to immediately pave the way for the officer to be returned.

"The Framers of the Constitution and Congress intended the interstate extradition process to be a swift, summary one in which the state into which a defendant travels promptly returns a fugitive as soon as the requesting state demands it," the state wrote in court filings last week.

Abbott cautioned he hasn't yet made a final decision on the extradition request. But his new filing said that any notion Minnesota could unilaterally enforce the extradition power was "doomed to fail." His filing also took shots at Walz for pardoning a man charged with sexually assaulting a minor.

"Equity favors those with clean hands," Abbott's lawyers wrote.

articles.title: US-Canada trade war heats up as Trump threatens to hike auto tariffs
articles.summary: Mark Carney accused Trump of wanting to "destroy" Canada's auto industry, and said he would only resume trade talks if the US comes with the "right attitude".
articles.body:
President Donald Trump has threatened to hike US tariffs on automobiles originating in Canada, as the trade war between the two neighbours continues to heat up.

Trump said on Monday that he will increase tariffs on Canadian cars and trucks, as well as auto parts, from 25% to 50% as of 1 January.

It comes after US-Canada trade talks collapsed late last week, with each side accusing the other of making unreasonable last-minute demands.

Late on Monday, Canada officials announced a news conference on Tuesday where they would outline how the country would respond to the trade war and work to "protect and support Canadian workers and businesses during these challenging times".

The news conference at 11:00 ET (16:00 BST) will include government leaders in business, finance and economic development.

Earlier in the day, Prime Minister Mark Carney called Trump's latest levy threat unsurprising and accused the president of wanting to destroy Canada's auto industry. He added that Canada is ready to resume talks only if the US comes with the "right attitude".

The war of words followed several US and Canadian officials saying that talks were suspended with no set date to resume.

Canada walked away from trade negotiations late on Friday night, moments before a US-imposed deadline that would add a 50% levy on nearly $20bn (C$28bn; £14bn) of Canadian imports.

The collapse in talks marked a significant change in tone from earlier in the week, when both sides appeared optimistic that a new US-Canada trade deal could be reached.

Canadian officials have said the US introduced last-minute demands that were "unacceptable", including a clause limiting which countries Canada could sign trade deals with.

US officials, meanwhile, said it was Canada that introduced last-minute changes.

"They wanted more," US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in an interview with CNBC on Monday.

The breakdown led to growing tensions as both sides publicly dug in their heels.

On Monday, Trump's tariff threats to Canada's auto industry followed Carney declaring the country would counter his levies with reciprocal tariffs on US goods "dollar for dollar".

'Half my business will be gone' - firms in Canada and US fear trade war

How Canada could hit back to hurt the US economy - and Trump

Trump says Canada wants 'benefits' of being US state after trade talks collapse

Carney said he was focused on supporting Canadian businesses impacted by new 50% US tariffs after the Friday deadline expired, as well as building infrastructure to diversify Canada's trade, which historically has relied heavily on the US.

Carney announced funding of C$11bn ($7.95bn; £5.83bn) to build six icebreakers at a Quebec shipyard for the Canadian Coast Guard that will replace its medium and heavy ageing fleet.

The icebreakers will be used to open winter shipping routes through Canada's northern and Atlantic waters.

Meanwhile, Ontario's outspoken premier, Doug Ford, whose province is home to Canada's auto manufacturing industry, responded to Trump's tariffs and threats by telling the US president to "kiss my ass".

Ford also suggested that Canada should charge the US extra for its oil and gas, as well as electricity and critical minerals, adding that he will be speaking to Carney on ways to "fight back".

His comments appeared to catch the attention of Trump, who in a Truth Social post accused Ford of "bluster" and wrote: "Someone should get these clowns to 'fall in line' or, the consequences for Canada will be far WORSE!".

Canada accounts for 60% of total US crude oil imports and close to 100% of US natural gas exports, according to Canadian government data.

Businesses on both sides have warned that they stand to be hurt by the new wave of US tariffs on Canada, as well as the retaliatory tariffs that Canada plans to impose on 8 September.

In Portland, Oregon, Mike Roach and Kim Osgood, owners of Paloma Clothing say the price of one of their best-selling items - specially designed pillows made in Canada - could shoot up by around 50% to $90. For now, they are holding out on keeping the prices steady, hoping that the "tariff problem" is worked out soon, said Roach.

"It would be one thing if we had three months' notice - that would be something you could plan around, do some work with the vendors," he said. "But when it happens literally overnight you're really stuck."

The rapidly escalating trade war is also raising questions about the other country in North America - Mexico - and the trade pact between the three neighbours known as the USMCA.

Both Canada and Mexico have said they want the USMCA extended for another 16 years, but the US has said it will not renew in its current form. The pact underpins $1.6tn in North American Trade.

Escalating trade tensions mean "the risk of the USMCA unravelling has increased", experts from the Oxford Economics forecasting firm warned on Monday. That, in turn, "would plunge Canada into recession and leave it on a permanently lower growth path".

Carney faces crucial test after walking away from Trump's deal
