articles.title: More than 70,000 social and affordable homes to be built across England over 10 years
articles.summary: Funding has been granted to Greater Manchester, the West Midlands and West Yorkshire as well as £6bn for London.
articles.body:
Ministers have announced where more than 70,000 social and affordable homes will be built in England over the next 10 years as part of an initial allocation of almost £10bn in a bid to address the housing crisis.

Funding has been granted to Greater Manchester, the West Midlands, West Yorkshire, South Yorkshire, North East England, and Liverpool. An additional £6bn was previously announced for London.

It is the first part of a wider plan to build 300,000 social and affordable homes, under the government's £39bn social housebuilding programme.

Housing charities welcomed the news but said it was still not enough to meet demand, while the Conservatives said it was an "unfunded spending commitment".

Social housing provides affordable homes at a low cost, managed by social landlords. It includes affordable rented properties as well as low-cost home ownership, such as shared ownership, and can be provided by local authorities and housing associations.

Earlier this year, before he became prime minister, Andy Burnham had called for the entire £39bn affordable housing budget for England to be spent on homes for social rent - which means the cost of the unit is about half that of market rents, and there are strict criteria for who can apply for it.

"I would actually devote all of it to social housing," Burnham told The Social Housing Podcast in May.

But of the new homes announced on Monday, 60% would be for social rent.

Housing Minister Matthew Pennycook told BBC Breakfast he did not accept Burnham had failed to meet his previous commitment, saying the government had taken a "pragmatic approach" and wants to "get money out the door".

He said the next tranche of funding would be more focused on council houses - which are usually also classed as homes for social rent.

It is understood ministers decided against giving councils more of the funding announced in the first tranche because they did not believe councils would be in a position to build the required number of social homes.

Under Labour, homeless figures have continued to rise to record levels and data released earlier this month suggested 177,530 children were homeless in temporary accommodation.

Natasha, who has been living in a hotel in Milton Keynes for the last four months with her son Zayd, is one of those waiting for a permanent home.

The 22-year-old spent the final months of her pregnancy and the first weeks of her son's life living in a hotel.

She told BBC's Your Voice she has no idea how long she will be expected to stay there but was told it would only be temporary.

"I'm just scared when he gets older, when he starts crawling around, I can't even allow him to crawl in such a place like that because it's so dirty," she says.

While pregnant, Natasha says her room became infested with ants, which she repeatedly reported before eventually being moved into another room.

While Natasha has her own bathroom, she shares a kitchen with around 60 other residents. She says the hotel is home to a mix of people, not just mothers and babies, and that she does not always feel safe using the shared space with Zayd.

Natasha describes living there as feeling "like a prison". She says visitors are not allowed, meaning friends and family can not come to help her with her five-week-old boy.

She is one of the 1.34 million households on social housing waiting lists as of March 2025, the latest government figures.

London will see the largest share of funding, although no figure has been given for how many homes will be built in the capital.

Ministers said Monday's allocation was the first stage of the 10-year programme and more than £16bn remains to be allocated outside London.

Housing Secretary Angela Rayner suggested some of the new homes will be built by councils, saying she and the prime minister were "doing everything we can to get councils building once again".

Speaking on a visit to a housing development in south-east London, she told the BBC she understood the "frustration of people who are in temporary accommodation at the moment or on one of those waiting lists".

But she insisted that she and the prime minister "are doing everything we can to get councils building once again".

Burnham had previously promised "the biggest council house building programme since the post-war period", but the announcement stops short of clarifying how the funding will be split between council homes and those provided by housing associations.

In the 1950s, councils were building almost 200,000 new council homes a year, but half of councils do not currently own or build their own homes.

In 2024 to 2025, around 65,000 new affordable homes were completed in England. Of those, there were just over 12,000 built for social rent - the highest since 2013 to 2014.

Organisations such as the National Housing Federation and homeless charities have previously agreed that at least 90,000 social homes would need to be built each year to meet demand.

Charlie Berry, policy manager at housing charity Shelter, said the announcement was "not near the level we need to truly tackle that backlog and end homelessness".

But she said it was a "significant improvement", and added she would "love" Rayner to commit to a target of how many socially rented homes will be built annually.

Conservative shadow housing secretary Sir James Cleverly described the announcement as "sleight of hand", saying: "The small print shows homes won't have to be delivered until 2039."

He said: "Fewer homes will be delivered than previous programmes in this Parliament as social rent is more expensive. Labour have scaled back their affordable housing programme and expect us to thank them for it."

The Conservatives have said they would end the provision of social housing for foreign nationals in England if they win power at the next election which they estimated would "free up" 228,144 homes for "British families".

On Monday, Reform UK announced similar plans to prioritise British-born workers under 35 when allocating social housing if it were to enter government.

Liberal Democrat housing spokesperson Gideon Amos welcomed parts of the government's plan, but said the plan for more social rent homes "won't cut it" and a programme is needed that "meets the scale of the challenge".

As well as the promise and funding to build more social homes, the Labour government pledged to build 1.5 million homes by 2029.

So far Labour is not on track to meet that target.

BBC Verify has been tracking the target using government statistics on the number of Energy Performance Certificates (EPC) issued by each local authority. Each newly created dwelling must have an EPC by law, making it the most timely indicator of new homes being built.

The latest EPC data suggests about 203,000 new homes were delivered in England in the 12 months ending June 2026. To reach the government's target of 1.5 million homes over five years, there would need to be at least 300,000.

'Each empty home shows there is a problem' - housing leaders call for action

'There are dozens of empty homes but families like mine are living in limbo'

Reform says it will prioritise British-born workers for social housing

articles.title: Wife of active-duty Army sergeant deported amid Trump's immigration campaign
articles.summary: An advocacy group says some military families are now "living in the shadows."
articles.body:
The wife of an Army sergeant and mother of a 6-year-old was deported on Monday.

Army Sgt. Hedar Leonel Turcios Juarez confirmed that his wife, Cristy Maryori Villafranca Trejo, was deported to Honduras. Turcios's wife's deportation comes as Trump's immigration crackdown impacts active-duty military spouses.

Turcios Juarez previously told ABC News that ICE officers detained Villafranca outside a Walmart in July as the couple's young daughter watched. Villafranca left Honduras in 2016 due to violent crime in the country, her husband said.

After attending high school in the U.S., he joined the military and became a U.S. citizen in 2024 after a nine-month deployment to the Middle East. Then he began pursuing citizenship for his wife, hoping his service would help expedite her naturalization process, he said.

"She's been a very supportive wife since the first day that I decided to join the military. I was deployed for nine months. She took care of my family," Turcios said of his spouse when she was detained. "She's not a threat to anybody. We're just trying to keep our family together."

The Department of Homeland Security confirmed the removal of Cristy Maryori Villafranca-Trejo, the wife of an army sergeant.

"On August 24, Cristy Maryori Villafranca-Trejo, an illegal alien from Honduras, was removed from the United States in accordance with our laws," a spokesperson for DHS said in a statement.

"On July 11, ICE conducted a targeted immigration enforcement operation to arrest Cristy Maryori Villafranca-Trejo, an illegal alien from Honduras," the spokesperson added. "Villafranca-Trejo illegally entered the United States in 2016 and was released into the country under the Obama administration."

Judge strikes down Trump administration policy that suspended immigrant visas for 75 countries, reinstating evaluations

Turcios' family is hardly alone. President Donald Trump's mass deportation campaign has swept up more than 50 parents and spouses of service members during his second term, with at least six deported, according to an investigation by the Associated Press.

Danitza James, CEO of Repatriate Our Patriots, which works with Families United to help active-duty service members and veterans reunite their families, said that, beyond providing legal representation, the organization's only other strategy has been to call Congress to request help.

She said she is currently working with eight active-duty service members and one veteran whose family members have been detained as of Aug. 20. ABC News spoke with two of the families that she is working to unite.

Trump admin sends 1st deportation flight to Haiti since ending temporary protected status

The cases complicate one of the administration's central arguments for its aggressive expansion of immigration enforcement. Trump has repeatedly said ICE is targeting the "worst of the worst," and has described immigrants who entered the U.S. illegally as "animals" and "dangerous criminals" that should not be in the country.

An ABC News review of state and federal records did not find criminal records for any of the military spouses named in this story in the states where they live.

"She's been a very supportive wife since the first day that I decided to join the military. I was deployed for nine months. She took care of my family," Turcios said of his spouse. "She's not a threat to anybody. We're just trying to keep our family together."

Pregnant woman has been held for weeks following immigration lawyer scam, family says

The Trump administration's detention of undocumented spouses and parents of active-duty service members comes as the U.S. is at war with Iran, leaving troops without the support of their families and shifting their focus away from their military careers, advocacy groups say. Some have been forced to take leave from duty to care for their children in their spouses' absence, according to advocacy groups and families ABC News interviewed.

"There are so many military families of active-duty service members that are living in the shadows of this immigration machine, that is putting them in fear of seeking resources and asking for help, while their service member is actively serving our country, and sacrificing for our nation," said James of Repatriate Our Patriots.

Military service has long been a pathway to citizenship

For decades, military families have occupied a protected corner of the immigration system, according to the National Military Family Association. Under policies embraced by Republican and Democratic administrations, the undocumented parents and spouses of service members have generally been shielded from deportation.

Military recruiters have also long promoted military service as a pathway to citizenship, including through programs which can allow undocumented relatives of troops to remain in the country while applying for a green card and work authorization.

The bargain extends to troops themselves. Green card holders can join the U.S. military and troops can apply for naturalization after a year of honorable service, an incentive that stretches back to the Civil War. During World War I, Congress went further, streamlining the citizenship process for troops whose enlistment could effectively mean automatic citizenship.

Virginia woman says ICE agent pointed gun at her, denies trying to run over agents

"Having a family member in the military is not a free pass to violate our nation's laws," a DHS spokesperson said in response to the recent arrest by ICE of the father of an active-duty sailor for alleged immigration violations. "Military service by an immediate relative does not automatically grant parole, lawful status, or immunity from immigration enforcement."

Racial and ethnic minorities are making up a growing share of the military. In the Army, the Pentagon's largest service by far, Hispanic recruits grew from about 19% of new enlistees in 2020 to nearly 27% last year, according to internal service data reviewed by ABC News.

Naturalizations through military service have also more than tripled over roughly the same period, rising from about 4,500 in 2020 to 16,000 in 2024, according to Department of Homeland Security data. The Philippines, Mexico, Jamaica and Nigeria were among the leading countries of origin for troops who became U.S. citizens through their service.

Turcios left Honduras in 2014, also to escape violence in the country, he said. After attending high school in the U.S. he joined the military and became a U.S. citizen in 2024 after a nine-month deployment to the Middle East. Then he began pursuing citizenship for his wife, hoping his service would help expedite her naturalization process, he said.

ACLU sues DHS over 'inhumane conditions' at nation's largest immigration detention facility

Instead, Villafranca, undocumented spouses and parents of many other active-duty military personnel have been forced into detention, according to lawyers, advocacy groups and military families.

Villafranca relayed allegedly inhumane conditions in Camp East Montana, according to her husband. The facility is the country's largest detention center, which sits on land formerly used for Japanese-American internment camps during World War II.

Turcios said his wife had to wear the same clothes for about four days. Access to clean clothing remained an issue until he reached out to Rep. Veronica Escobar, D- Texas, who sent an inquiry to ICE regarding Villafranca's lack of clean clothing. Turcios said that after a few weeks, they finally fixed the issue.

​Army Staff Sgt. Alexis Jaramillo has served in the military for 11 years and is currently stationed at Fort Polk, Louisiana. His wife, Maisa Lopes Eliaser, came to the U.S. from São Paulo, Brazil, in 2019 on a tourist visa, which she had overstayed while Jaramillo was helping her pursue citizenship.

She was taken into custody in front of Jaramillo, who was dressed in uniform, and their five-year-old son during an appointment to be interviewed to get her green card.

Lopes Eliaser spent two days in Pickens County Jail in Georgia before being transferred to the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center, where she slept in a large room with approximately 80 people for about six weeks, her husband said.

​On July 13, Lopes Eliaser said ICE officers put her on a bus to the Alexandria International Airport in Louisiana. She was then flown to Bogotá, Colombia, where the plane stopped before its final destination, Brazil. During the layover, Lopes Eliaser called her husband using someone else's phone, he said.

Jaramillo said he had been communicating with Sen. Mark Kelly, a Navy veteran, about his wife's case before she was taken to the airport. When Lopes Eliaser disappeared from the detainee-tracking app that Jaramillo was checking, he contacted Kelly again to ask for help bringing her home.

"Maisa's case is an example of this administration's focus on targeting the loved ones of those who've stepped up to serve our country. It's wrong and makes no sense at all," Kelly wrote in a statement to ABC News.

Kelly's office told ABC News that his casework team established communications with the ICE field office and kept Jaramillo updated.

DHS did not respond to a request for comment on Eliaser's case at the time.

Jaramillo credits Kelly for contacting ICE and getting Lopes Eliaser eventually returned to the U.S. When she landed in Brazil, she was flown back to the Alexandria International Airport without ever stepping off the airplane. Jaramillo and Lopes Eliaser were reunited and are currently together at their home in Louisiana.

Padres minor league coach detained by ICE at El Paso airport

​"That was a nightmare. That was a really, really nightmare," Jaramillo said. "I'm never going to explain best how difficult it was and still is."

​While Jaramillo and Lopes Eliaser are now united, they are still dealing with the aftermath of her detention and deportation. Jaramillo had to take leave to care for his son and fight to get his wife back. Now that his wife is back home, he said he will return to service on Monday.

Since Lopes Eliaser was first detained, Jaramillo said he has incurred more than $7,000 in legal fees and costs associated with submitting paperwork, approximately equal to over a month's pay.

​Jaramillo said his wife is still experiencing health issues from the conditions of detention, which he said were crowded and where she also lacked access to clean clothing. Jarmillo said he took her to see a doctor Thursday.

Petition filed days before ICE detainee's death cited medical conditions while seeking his release

​James said that many of the other cases of active-duty military service members' families being detained have involved members of Congress making calls to reunite families.

Kelly has publicly been involved with two other cases of military families targeted by the Trump administration for deportation.

​In a letter sent Aug. 9 to DHS, the Defense Department and the Department of Veterans Affairs, congressional Democrats wrote that they will investigate whether the Pentagon and DHS are coordinating to deport military service members and their families.

​"The best way to bring change to this is to the legislative or policy, because this should not be a phone call. This should not be a one-case change," James said. "This is clearly impacting more than 50 military spouses and cases across the board, and there needs to be a change that is codified."

articles.title: UK drone factories may face attacks from 'unknown sources', says former Russian minister
articles.summary: The comments on BBC Newsnight come after the UK announced it has agreed to hand over blueprints for British-made missile components to Ukraine.
articles.body:
A Russian former deputy foreign minister has said there might be a "semi-military" response against UK drone factories by "unknown sources" over the sharing of blueprints for British-made cruise missile components .

Andrei Fedorov's comments on BBC Newsnight come as UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced plans to travel to the US next month with European leaders to lobby President Donald Trump on Ukraine's defence needs.

Burnham's trip, should it go ahead, would be his first to the US since becoming prime minister.

"Leaving today, I'm quite clear what I need to do in the next few weeks," he said following his visit to Ukraine on Monday, during which he promised to continue pressuring Russia.

The UK has agreed to hand over blueprints for British-made components for the Scalp missile , a French version of the UK's Storm Shadow cruise missile. The blueprints will allow Ukraine to produce the long-range weapon domestically.

Fedorov, a pro-Kremlin commentator who frequently appears on Russian television, said Putin was facing "serious" pressure "to undertake certain measures against UK". Asked on BBC Newsnight where the pressure was coming from, Fedorov responded "public opinion polls, it's coming from journalists, from mass media".

Asked what a "semi-military" response might look like, Fedorov said: "It could take the form of something might happen with enterprises, with factories which are producing drones for Ukraine.

"They could be attacked not by Russia, but by from unknown sources."

The comments are in line with those made by Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov on Monday, when he criticised the UK's decision to share the missile blueprints. Peskov said it prevented "even the slightest progress" towards achieving peace.

He told reporters on Monday that the Russian military was already gathering data to locate any missile production sites to destroy them.

"Britain is involved in this war on the side of the Kyiv regime. Britain methodically and regularly adds fuel to the fire," he added.

In response, Burnham said: "Who started the fire? That's the question, isn't it?"

Burnham's visit to Ukraine was his first official international trip. He met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Kyiv and chaired his first meeting of the "coalition of the willing", set up by the UK and France under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.

Burnham has been reaffirming the UK's support for Ukraine in the wake of escalating Russian strikes in recent weeks - including one last week on a shopping centre that killed at least 16 people.

Ukraine has been relying on American supplies of the Patriot interceptor missiles, which are used to combat Russia's ballistic missiles , but stockpiles are running low due to the war in Iran, leaving Ukraine vulnerable to Russian attacks.

Zelensky has said he is hoping to secure 300 patriot missiles ahead of winter, when Russia is likely to increase its attacks on energy infrastructure, as it has done in past years.

In the interview with Bloomberg, Burnham said he felt "really confident" that the issue was "fixable". But he pointed out that it wasn't only the US who could supply Ukraine with Patriots.

"There are other players who could help in the mix who we have influence with," he said. "It's probably going to be a solution that involves a lot of layers and a lot of negotiation."

In July this year, three weeks after offering Ukraine the right to produce Patriots itself, Trump backtracked, saying : "We have not agreed to that. We're talking about it. But it's a hard thing to give away, that kind of technology."

"These weapons are incredible. We have to be very careful about letting somebody build them," Trump told a cabinet meeting.

In a joint statement after the meeting in Ukraine, Burnham and co-chairs French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the group would aim to strength Kyiv's air defences "as a matter or urgent priority".

They also condemned Moscow's "systemic and escalating strikes against Ukraine's cities, critical infrastructure and civilians" and pledged to "constrain Russia's war chest through sanctions and actions against the shadow fleet".

In a statement ahead of the visit, Burnham said: "On Ukraine's 35th anniversary of independence, the Ukrainian people should be in no doubt: the UK is behind you today and for as long as it takes.

"I am proud of the contribution our country has made to Ukraine and I want the Ukrainian people to hear it directly from me that our support will not waver. After all, Ukraine's security is our security."

He said the friendship Ukraine shared with the UK would "long outlast Russia's illegal war", adding: "Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve. We will not back down until there is a just and lasting peace."

Burnham vows support for Ukraine despite 'outrageous threats' from Russia

articles.title: Whisky barrel bought for £130 goes on sale at £270,000
articles.summary: Pensioner Angus Kerr bought the cask of Glenrothes single malt in 1971 for £130 as an investment.
articles.body:
A whisky barrel purchased for £130 is to go on sale for £270,000.

Surrey pensioner Angus Kerr said he had bought the Glenrothes single malt in 1971 as an investment, hoping it would help pay for his children's school fees.

He said it was now worth an "unbelievable" sum, as the barrel was the oldest of its kind known to be in existence.

"I don't drink scotch," Kerr said. "If I did, I would be looking around for something that was £18, no more. That's my sort of level."

Kerr, a former commodities trader, said he had made the purchase after hearing about a company selling barrels of new-fill whisky.

"I thought at least I can go for a swim in it if it all goes belly up," he told BBC Radio Surrey .

Kerr said he had hoped to sell the barrel five years later for a profit, but the company went bust and he lost contact with them.

"I just threw my hands in the air and thought, 'OK, that was silly'," he added.

However, a few years later, the 81-year-old was contacted out of the blue by a Glaswegian company, which said he owed them money for storing the barrel.

After getting waylaid by "business, kids and life in general", Kerr said he had only recently contacted broker Mark Littler to try to sell the barrel, which contains enough for approximately 287 bottles.

Kerr said the tasting experts had declared the 57-year-old whisky "absolutely fantastic".

"It could have lost its alcohol content or ended up being very oaky and horrible, so it's very fortunate," he added.

"What we need to find is Elon Musk, [Jeff] Bezos or someone for who £270,000 is just spare change to them."

On how he would spend the proceeds, Kerr said he would not have any "difficulty finding a home for the money" with his children and eight grandchildren.

"But it goes pretty quickly these days," he added.

paragraphs: A whisky barrel purchased for £130 is to go on sale for £270,000.
Surrey pensioner Angus Kerr said he had bought the Glenrothes single malt in 1971 as an investment, hoping it would help pay for his children's school fees.
He said it was now worth an "unbelievable" sum, as the barrel was the oldest of its kind known to be in existence.
"I don't drink scotch," Kerr said. "If I did, I would be looking around for something that was £18, no more. That's my sort of level."
Kerr, a former commodities trader, said he had made the purchase after hearing about a company selling barrels of new-fill whisky.
"I thought at least I can go for a swim in it if it all goes belly up," he told BBC Radio Surrey .
Kerr said he had hoped to sell the barrel five years later for a profit, but the company went bust and he lost contact with them.
"I just threw my hands in the air and thought, 'OK, that was silly'," he added.
However, a few years later, the 81-year-old was contacted out of the blue by a Glaswegian company, which said he owed them money for storing the barrel.

After getting waylaid by "business, kids and life in general", Kerr said he had only recently contacted broker Mark Littler to try to sell the barrel, which contains enough for approximately 287 bottles.
Kerr said the tasting experts had declared the 57-year-old whisky "absolutely fantastic".
"It could have lost its alcohol content or ended up being very oaky and horrible, so it's very fortunate," he added.
"What we need to find is Elon Musk, [Jeff] Bezos or someone for who £270,000 is just spare change to them."
On how he would spend the proceeds, Kerr said he would not have any "difficulty finding a home for the money" with his children and eight grandchildren.
"But it goes pretty quickly these days," he added.

articles.title: US government wants companies to pay more while filing H-1B visas, what the revised fee hike proposal says
articles.summary: Tech News News: The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has unveiled a proposal that would dramatically increase costs for employers who are sponsoring foreign w.
articles.body: The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has unveiled a proposal that would dramatically increase costs for employers who are sponsoring foreign workers under the H-1B visa program. According to the draft rule published for public inspection, companies filing cap-subject H-1B petitions would face a new standalone fee of $103,265 per petition, along with the existing charges. DHS says that the measure is aimed to recovering immigration system costs across multiple agencies.What the revised H-1b visa proposal actually saysAccording to the notice, DHS "proposes to establish a $103,265 fee, payable at the time of filing, for all H-1B cap-subject petitions, including those eligible for the advanced degree exemption, which would be imposed in addition to all other applicable fees or payments." In plain terms, this isn't a replacement for existing H-1B costs â it's a new, standalone charge stacked on top of everything employers already pay to file a petition.The fee would apply to the 65,000 visas issued under the regular annual cap as well as the 20,000 visas reserved for foreign workers holding a qualifying US master's degree or higher. It would not apply to cap-exempt petitions, which cover many roles at universities, nonprofit research organizations, and government research institutions.How DHS landed on $103,265 feeThe figure isn't arbitrary. DHS calculated it by dividing the total costs it wants to recover â $8,777,488,035 â by a projected annual filing volume of 85,000 cap-subject petitions, arriving at $103,264.57, which the agency then rounded to the nearest $5 increment consistent with its past fee-setting practice.The agency argues this approach is justified because H-1B petitioners are, in its words, an applicant pool that is "most willing and able to pay an additional fee" compared with other immigration benefit requestors, given that employers are already required to pay a certified prevailing wage to the workers they sponsor.Separate from â and stackable with â the $100,000 proclamation feeThis proposal is legally distinct from the $100,000 payment imposed last year under Presidential Proclamation 10973, which was struck down in June 2026 by a federal judge in Massachusetts (a ruling now under appeal at the First Circuit). DHS is explicit that the new $103,265 fee relies on different statutory authority â primarily sections 286(j) and (m) of the Immigration and Nationality Act â rather than the president's proclamation power used for the earlier fee.Notably, the rule states that if the proclamation's payment requirement is ever reinstated through the appeals process, employers subject to both would have to pay both amounts â the $100,000 proclamation fee and the new $103,265 rule-based fee â on top of each other. The proclamation itself is due to expire in September unless extended, and DHS notes this new rule is intended to take its place going forward.Impact on employersDHS argues that employers sponsoring Hâ1B workers generally have the resources to absorb the fee, noting median annual wages of $133,000 for Hâ1B employees. However, the government acknowledges the fee may reduce filings, particularly among smaller firms. Public comments on the proposal are open until 30 days after publication in the Federal Register (August 25, 2026).Where the money would goUnlike most past USCIS fee increases, which funded USCIS alone, this proposal spreads the roughly $8.8 billion in projected annual revenue across six federal agencies involved in different parts of the immigration system:* USCIS â 34.2% ($3.0 billion), covering adjudications, staffing increases, and IT modernization* EOIR (the Justice Department's immigration courts) â 33.7% ($2.96 billion), funding roughly 8,400 new positions including immigration judges* DOL â 13.8% ($1.21 billion), covering labor certification and wage-enforcement functions* ICE â 11.9% ($1.05 billion), covering vetting and the Student and Exchange Visitor Program* DOS â 5.5% ($484 million), covering consular vetting and fraud-prevention systems* CBP â 0.9% ($76.2 million), covering biometric entry-exit matchingDHS frames this interagency cost-sharing as consistent with its statutory authority to recover the "full costs" of administering the lawful immigration system â not just the direct cost of processing a single petition, but the broader web of vetting, enforcement, and court functions connected to it.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: Rescuers find no trace of 22 missing crew days after cargo ship sinks in Bay of Bengal
articles.summary: Rescuers searching for 22 missing sailors have found no trace of their Panama-flagged cargo ship after the vessel sank in the Bay of Bengal last week, the In...
articles.body:
NEW DELHI (AP) — Rescuers searching for 22 missing sailors have found no trace of their Panama-flagged cargo ship after the vessel sank in the Bay of Bengal last week, the Indian Coast Guard said Tuesday.

Search aircraft and ships on Tuesday were scouring the area where the cargo ship MV Ocean Winner reportedly sunk Saturday about 276 miles (444 kilometers) from the Paradip coast of India's eastern Odisha state.

The joint search by the Indian Coast Guard and Indian Navy has been complicated by the area's exceptionally deep waters and found only an oil slick and two life rafts near the vessel's last known position, officials said.

The lack of wreckage has hampered efforts to determine the cause of the sinking and where to focus search operations, authorities said.

The vessel transporting iron ore to China was carrying 24 crew members, including 20 Chinese nationals, three Myanmar nationals and one Bangladeshi, according to the coast guard.

Two Chinese crew members were rescued Saturday following a distress call from the ship, the coast guard said.

articles.title: Man dies in crash after Stratford-upon-Avon police pursuit
articles.summary: Two women are also hurt and one remains in hospital in critical condition.
articles.body:
A man has died and two women have been injured in a crash after a police pursuit near Stratford-upon-Avon.

Officers tried to stop a black Audi on Birmingham Road shortly before 17:30 BST on Monday but the driver failed to pull over, Warwickshire Police said.

A pursuit began and 15 minutes later the Audi crashed into a white Ford Puma, the force added, with the Audi's 19-year-old male driver confirmed dead at the scene by paramedics.

The driver of the Ford, a woman, was seriously injured and remains in hospital in critical condition, while injuries to a second woman - her passenger - were serious but not believed to be life-threatening. An investigation by the police watchdog is under way.

Officers said after failing to stop, the Audi made off in the direction of the A46 before travelling back towards Stratford on the A439 Warwick Road where the crash occurred.

A number of other cars were damaged during the pursuit, police said.

Warwick Road was closed on Monday from the Marraway roundabout to its junction with Ingon Lane and Sand Barn Lane, with the stretch remaining shut on Tuesday morning.

A spokesperson for West Midlands Ambulance Service said paramedics found four patients in total at the scene.

They included a man who was in a critical condition to whom crews gave advanced life support.

"Despite their best efforts, it became clear that nothing more could be done to save him and he was confirmed deceased by ambulance staff at the scene," the spokesperson said.

A woman who was driving the second car suffered life-threatening injuries, the ambulance service confirmed, and was taken to hospital in a critical condition. She was said by the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) to be in her 70s.

A female passenger in the vehicle was also seriously hurt and taken to hospital, although her condition was not thought by the ambulance service to be life-threatening.

Injuries to another patient from the car were not believed to be serious.

Supt Steve Flavell said: "Our thoughts are with the families of everyone involved in this collision... at this extremely difficult time.

"We made a mandatory referral to the IOPC because a death had occurred following police contact.

"They have declared an independent investigation and we will co-operate fully with their investigation."

The IOPC said the investigation was at an early stage and confirmed its officials attended the police's post-incident operation to gather information.

"We understand the driver of a black Audi A3 failed to stop for police and was then pursued for around six minutes before the vehicle was involved in a collision with a car being driven by a member of the public," a spokesperson said.

"We are also appealing for any car footage of the pursuit that other motorists may have recorded. Our investigators can be contacted at 0300 303 5609 or by email: WarwickRoadPursuit@policeconduct.gov.uk

"We have met with the families of the driver and the seriously injured woman to explain our role and will keep them regularly updated throughout our investigation, which is at an early stage."

Manuela Perteghella, Liberal Democrat MP for Stratford-on-Avon, said the incdent was "incredibly tragic".

"My thoughts are with the families of all those impacted. We must now let the investigation take its course."

Works were carried out on Warwick Road two years ago, aimed at reducing the number of crashes in the area.

Warwickshire County Council added a one-way system, lowered the speed limit and implemented a protected turning lane at the Ingon Lane junction.

Street lighting was also boosted to improve visibility for crossing pedestrians at Fisherman's Car Park.

Road set to reopen after being closed for months

articles.title: BPSC exam row, 'dogs bark' remark: What has triggered fresh student protests in Bihar
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Chaotic scenes unfolded in Biharâs Patna on Tuesday as protesting students clashed with police during a massive protest over alleged irregu.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Chaotic scenes unfolded in Biharâs Patna on Tuesday as protesting students clashed with police during a massive protest over alleged irregularities in the 70th BPSC examination.The protest was met with a heavy police deployment, with barricades erected to stop the students from marching.Police also used water cannons as protesters attempted to push past the barricades.Later, the Samrat Choudhary-led government claimed it had addressed âalmost all issuesâ raised by the students. The protesters, however, said several long-standing demands remained unresolved and continued their agitation.The students marched from Gandhi Maidan towards Raj Bhavan.The protesting students also broke the barricades in bid to gherao chief minister's residence.The protest has also brought into focus delays in recruitment examinations, the proposed format of the Teacher Recruitment Examination-4 (TRE-4), alleged paper leaks and demands for greater transparency in Bihar's recruitment system.Govt says students' issues have been addressedBihar education minister Mithilesh Tiwari said the government had resolved the issues raised by the students and maintained that its doors remained open for further dialogue."All the issues over which the students were staging a sit-in have been resolved. It is not as if the student agitation was the sole reason for this; it is the government's very intent to resolve the problems faced by our youth in a timely manner. We have addressed every issue raised by the youth. I was surprised to hear a person who has never even taken a board exam offering suggestions on examinations. That is why I would say to Tejashwi Yadav to enroll in a Bihar government school, pass the tenth-grade exam, and then come back to offer us suggestions on examinations," Tiwari said.The minister said that almost all the demands had been met and invited students to approach the government with any remaining concerns."We have met almost all the students' demands. For any students who wish to convey further points to the government, the doors for dialogue remain wide open. Let the students come, talk, and get their issues resolved; the government belongs to them," he said.However, the protesters said their concerns had not been fully addressed and that problems related to the education system, examination paper leaks and delayed recruitment continued.'Do you need 1,800 years?' Students question recruitment delaysProtester Vikas Bhatt said the students were demanding improvements in Bihar's education system and action against repeated examination paper leaks."Our demand is that the education system in Bihar be improved. We are raising issues regarding the frequent exam paper leaks in the state. Look at the recruitment for librarians, it hasn't happened for 18 years; do you need 1,800 years? Whenever we stage a protest, they simply offer assurances and leave it at that. How can things go on like this? Three recruitment drives were announced through the BSSC, but it has been three years. We have repeatedly besieged the BSSC commission, demanding that the exam dates be announced. Despite this, they keep asking for 15 days' time. Apart from the BPSC, there isn't a single commission in Bihar that issues an annual calendar," Bhatt said.The students are demanding the cancellation of the 70th BPSC examination over allegations of irregularities and paper leaks.The agitation has also centred on the proposed TRE-4 examination. Students have opposed the proposal to conduct the examination in two phases across Bihar and are demanding that it be held in a single phase.They have also sought the immediate release of the official TRE-4 advertisement.Students break through barricades during Raj Bhavan marchAs the protest continued, students marched from Gandhi Maidan towards Raj Bhavan. Some protesters broke through police barricades and attempted to move towards the restricted area.Police used water cannons to disperse the crowd, while several protesters were detained.DSP Kamakhya Narayan Singh said the police would not allow the protesters to enter the restricted area, although he expressed hope that the ongoing talks between students and senior officials would lead to a resolution."We will stop them; we won't let them proceed further. However, the dialogue has been positive, and we hope the students will agree. They have raised several issues with the senior officials, and the outcome has been positive. So, I expect the turnout to be lower and that they will agree. If they don't, we will stop them right here. We won't allow them to enter the restricted area," Singh said.Congress leader Sushil Kumar, who was present at the protest site, said the government had failed to give assurances on several key demands."We want to state clearly that a single-stage examination must be implemented for TRE 4.0 at all costs, and negative marking should be abolished. There are numerous other issues as well, regarding the BPSC, BSSC, Sub-Inspector recruitment. The government has offered no assurances on any of these points. We have urged the Chief Minister to hold a dialogue; he should invite our delegation for talks. We have been on a hunger strike for nine days, yet no one is willing to listen to us. Just imagine, had the government engaged in dialogue, this situation would not have arisen. We are heading towards the Chief Minister's residence; the Chief Minister should hold talks, and our delegation will go there for the discussion," Kumar told news agency ANI.JD(U) says govt is serious about students' concernsJD(U) leader Shravan Kumar said the Bihar government was taking the concerns of students and job seekers seriously and was acting according to established rules and legal provisions."The government is taking the demands and concerns of students and job seekers seriously. Everything is being done for them in accordance with established rules, laws, and provisions. Bihar is the first state in the country to have made such large-scale recruitments across government departments," Kumar said.He also pointed to the government's employment target for the 2025-2030 period and urged young people not to be influenced by the opposition."It is Nitish Kumar's resolve to provide 10 million (1 crore) jobs and employment opportunities to the people of Bihar between 2025 and 2030. Recruitments are taking place in every sector, and vacancies are being announced in every department. I urge our youth to exercise patience and not fall for the opposition's ploys; they are not going to provide jobs. They merely intend to exploit your hard work and sweat to further their own political interests. Beware of them," he added.Tejashwi writes to Samrat ChoudharyMeanwhile, Bihar leader of opposition Tejashwi Yadav has written to chief minister Samrat Choudhary over the ongoing BPSC row, urging the government not to ignore the students' demands and to hold talks for an early resolution.Tejashwi has demanded that TRE-4 be conducted as a single examination across the state. He has also sought an end to what he described as discrimination against Hindi-speaking candidates in the BPSC Civil Services Main Examination and interview.The RJD leader has further demanded complete transparency in all competitive examinations, including those for Sub-Inspector, Constable, BSSC and BPSC recruitments.Among his other demands are a high-level independent inquiry into alleged irregularities in past examinations, strict action against recruitment mafias and time-bound schedules for all pending tests.He has specifically called for clear timelines for the BSSC Intermediate, CGL, ASO, BSO, Librarian and Accountant recruitment examinations.RJD scion Tejashwi remark also followed BPSC official's "dog-barking" remark. Bihar LoP also called for action for his remark referring to students.Bihar launches monthly student support campsAmid the continuing protests, the Bihar government on Tuesday launched the monthly 'Vidyarthi Sahyog Shivir' or student support camps to address students' grievances.The camps will be organised at educational institutions on the fourth Tuesday of every month, chief minister Samrat Choudhary said in a social media post."The Bihar government is launching Vidyarthi Sahyog Shivir starting today to ensure prompt resolution of students' grievances. These camps will be organised at educational institutions on the fourth Tuesday of every month," Choudhary wrote.The camps will allow students to raise their grievances directly with the concerned government officials. Students will also be able to register complaints online and track their status through the portal and Helpline 1100.The government's announcement comes as the student protest continues in Patna's Gardanibagh area, with the two sides offering sharply different views on whether the protesters' demands have been addressed.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

Just imagine, had the government engaged in dialogue, this situation would not have arisen. We are heading towards the Chief Minister's residence; the Chief Minister should hold talks, and our delegation will go there for the discussion," Kumar told news agency ANI.JD(U) says govt is serious about students' concernsJD(U) leader Shravan Kumar said the Bihar government was taking the concerns of students and job seekers seriously and was acting according to established rules and legal provisions."The government is taking the demands and concerns of students and job seekers seriously. Everything is being done for them in accordance with established rules, laws, and provisions. Bihar is the first state in the country to have made such large-scale recruitments across government departments," Kumar said.He also pointed to the government's employment target for the 2025-2030 period and urged young people not to be influenced by the opposition."It is Nitish Kumar's resolve to provide 10 million (1 crore) jobs and employment opportunities to the people of Bihar between 2025 and 2030. Recruitments are taking place in every sector, and vacancies are being announced in every department. I urge our youth to exercise patience and not fall for the opposition's ploys; they are not going to provide jobs. They merely intend to exploit your hard work and sweat to further their own political interests. Beware of them," he added.Tejashwi writes to Samrat ChoudharyMeanwhile, Bihar leader of opposition Tejashwi Yadav has written to chief minister Samrat Choudhary over the ongoing BPSC row, urging the government not to ignore the students' demands and to hold talks for an early resolution.Tejashwi has demanded that TRE-4 be conducted as a single examination across the state. He has also sought an end to what he described as discrimination against Hindi-speaking candidates in the BPSC Civil Services Main Examination and interview.The RJD leader has further demanded complete transparency in all competitive examinations, including those for Sub-Inspector, Constable, BSSC and BPSC recruitments.Among his other demands are a high-level independent inquiry into alleged irregularities in past examinations, strict action against recruitment mafias and time-bound schedules for all pending tests.He has specifically called for clear timelines for the BSSC Intermediate, CGL, ASO, BSO, Librarian and Accountant recruitment examinations.RJD scion Tejashwi remark also followed BPSC official's "dog-barking" remark. Bihar LoP also called for action for his remark referring to students.Bihar launches monthly student support campsAmid the continuing protests, the Bihar government on Tuesday launched the monthly 'Vidyarthi Sahyog Shivir' or student support camps to address students' grievances.The camps will be organised at educational institutions on the fourth Tuesday of every month, chief minister Samrat Choudhary said in a social media post."The Bihar government is launching Vidyarthi Sahyog Shivir starting today to ensure prompt resolution of students' grievances. These camps will be organised at educational institutions on the fourth Tuesday of every month," Choudhary wrote.The camps will allow students to raise their grievances directly with the concerned government officials. Students will also be able to register complaints online and track their status through the portal and Helpline 1100.The government's announcement comes as the student protest continues in Patna's Gardanibagh area, with the two sides offering sharply different views on whether the protesters' demands have been addressed.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Rajnath Singh approves transfer of DRDO missile technology to Indian defence industry
articles.summary: News News: NEW DELHI: Defence minister Rajnath Singh has approved the transfer of DRDO-developed technologies for all conventional missile systems to Indian defe.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Defence minister Rajnath Singh has approved the transfer of DRDO-developed technologies for all conventional missile systems to Indian defence companies for production within the country, the defence ministry said on Tuesday.The move is aimed at accelerating indigenous missile manufacturing, reducing import dependence and expanding the role of domestic companies in India's defence ecosystem.The ministry described the technology transfer as an "important milestone" in increasing industry participation and enabling the transition of missile systems from development to industrial production."The provision will enable successful transition of missile system development to industrial production, reflecting the continued efforts of DRDO (Defence Research and Development Organisation) to leverage the capabilities of the Indian industry for the development and manufacture of advanced defence systems," the ministry said.Under the initiative, Indian defence companies will be able to undertake production of DRDO-developed conventional missile technologies, subject to applicable qualifications, certifications and regulatory requirements.The government said the move is intended to strengthen India's domestic defence industrial base and expand manufacturing capabilities.The initiative will also create opportunities for Indian micro, small and medium enterprises and other technology partners to participate in missile production and related supply chains.The defence ministry said the initiative would increase domestic value addition while supporting the growth of India's defence manufacturing sector.DRDO will continue to work with Indian industry to facilitate the transfer and absorption of advanced defence technologies, the ministry said.

articles.title: Young care leavers dying early a 'national tragedy'
articles.summary: Those leaving care have a death rate around four times higher than the general population, a new review reveals.
articles.body:
Young adults who have left care have a death rate around four times higher than the general population, a new review shows.

Often left alone "with no safety net," the report says the consequences can be catastrophic.

On turning 18, people leaving care in England often lose "significant levers of support", the Government-commissioned report concluded, as it warned the so-called "care cliff" must be addressed.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4 Today , report co-author and broadcaster Ashley John-Baptiste, who grew up in care, called the deaths a national tragedy.

There were 112 deaths of care leavers aged 18 to 24 notified in 2025, which the review said equalled about 130 deaths per 100,000 care leavers.

John-Baptiste recalled his own experience of turning 18 and moving out of the last of four foster homes he'd lived in.

"I was made to live alone and work out how to be an adult," he said.

Unable to afford a bed frame, he says he slept on a mattress on the floor of his council flat and felt a deep sense of abandonment and isolation.

The report, co-authored by social worker Clare Chamberlain and commissioned by the Department for Education, found 18 appeared to be a significant turning point.

Of the deaths, 22 occurred at 18 – more than any other age in the range – which the review said was "strongly suggestive of the stark challenges and pressures" faced by these young people when they leave care.

Just over a third (40) of the care leavers were thought to have died by suicide, a rate the report said was potentially five times higher than that of the general population.

Other causes included murder, road traffic accidents and drug misuse, as well as potential mismanagement of medical conditions like diabetes.

The report calls for better ways to prepare young people for adulthood and an overhaul of the workforce supporting them.

The main source of support provided to young people who have left care comes through the framework of having a personal adviser (PA).

The review found that the support provided by PAs can "vary greatly from place to place" with a "huge variation" in quality of practice.

With minimum visiting requirements of once every two months, the authors say it is "not surprising" that some PAs they spoke to "hardly knew" the young person they were supporting.

The report is also critical of the housing and accommodation support given to young adults, saying it is often from a "profit-making arm of the service with no specific requirements for a therapeutic or social work discipline", which needs to be redressed.

The government says it is driving forward a national rollout of connected housing options for those leaving care, starting with £25 million this year.

It says this will "significantly increase" young people's chances of being offered a "home that provides them with community and connection rather than leaving them isolated in inappropriate accommodation".

Children's Minister Josh MacAlister said "enduring relationships" must become the "central obsession" of the care system.

"Care must build and not break the relationships that young people need, and this must be the new North Star," he added.

Izy Winter was put into care at 13. Now 25, she says she was let down at every stage.

"While I was in care I was cold, hungry and neglected," she says.

As a care leaver she experienced failures that left her feeling "invisible and unprotected".

Izy was living with an abusive partner, but welfare checks that should have picked up on this were not carried out correctly, she says.

"The person who was meant to check asked to meet me in the car park and got me to sign a piece of paper to say he'd been inside my home when he hadn't," she said.

Izy has ADHD and dyslexia and struggles with paperwork. Her support worker did not check that she was receiving all the financial support she was entitled to. By the time she was made aware, it was too late and she could not reclaim the money she had missed out on.

"I was really struggling financially and was so frustrated that even when I asked for help, I wasn't given it."

She says she is saddened, but not surprised, to read the new report.

"The recent findings reflect a reality that too many of us have lived through".

If you've been affected by the issues in this story, you can find information, advice and support from the BBC's Action Line . Anyone feeling emotionally distressed or suicidal can call Samaritans for free on 116 123 or visit samaritans.org in the UK.

articles.title: Record heatwaves kill more than 35,000 across Europe, toll expected to rise: Report
articles.summary: Europe News: At least 35,000 excess deaths have happened across Europe during four record-breaking heatwaves this summer, according to a report by the Guardian. Th.
articles.body: At least 35,000 excess deaths have happened across Europe during four record-breaking heatwaves this summer, according to a report by the Guardian. The actual toll is likely to be significantly higher, with August data still unavailable for several countries and heat-related deaths often taking weeks or months to formally identify.Germany, France and Spain alone have recorded more than 25,000 excess deaths. Germany has reported the highest toll, with the Robert Koch Institute estimating around 14,000 heat-related deaths between April 6 and August 9, the country's highest figure since records began.The consecutive heatwaves began in May and pushed temperatures to unprecedented levels across western Europe.France recorded its hottest national average day on record, while more than 500 French weather stations recorded temperatures above 40Â°C. Germany saw 46 stations cross 40Â°C in late June, while parts of Spain experienced prolonged temperatures above 42Â°C.Germany's toll was particularly severe in late June, when the Robert Koch Institute estimated that 9,600 people died during the week of June 22-28. The country's previous annual high for heat-related deaths was 8,900 in 2018, while normal summers typically see fewer than 2,000 such deaths.Spain's mortality monitoring system has attributed 4,947 deaths to heat since May, already surpassing the previous record of 4,520 recorded in 2022. In France, preliminary figures showed 7,300 excess deaths between late May and July 22, although the data covered only about 80% of total mortality and did not include August.Other countries have also reported significant increases. England's health security agency estimated that the May and June heatwaves were linked to 2,877 deaths. Belgium recorded 1,222 excess deaths during an 11-day period in June, while the Netherlands reported at least 900 additional deaths between June 22 and July 5. Modelling estimated another 1,070 excess deaths in Poland during the late-June heatwave.The figures are difficult to establish because heat is rarely recorded as the direct cause of death. Extreme temperatures can worsen existing cardiovascular, respiratory and kidney conditions, with the resulting heart attacks, strokes or organ failures recorded as the immediate causes of death.Experts expect the European death toll to rise as countries consolidate their figures.Italy, for instance, has not yet released a final national estimate, although modelling has suggested that between 5,000 and 8,000 heat-related deaths could eventually be recorded.Scientists have linked the increasingly frequent and intense heatwaves to human-driven global warming. The World Health Organisation said in May that heat-related mortality in its European region had risen by more than 30% over the past two decades and warned that the toll could increase further as the climate crisis intensifies and Europe's population ages.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Suffolk Wildlife Trust launches 'first-of-its-kind' nature survey
articles.summary: A wildlife group says "everyone can get involved with protecting nature" by taking part in research.
articles.body:
A wildlife trust has said it has launched a first-of-its-kind survey to help find out how people feel about nature and guide future conservation efforts.

The Suffolk Wildlife Trust (SWT), in collaboration with the University of Suffolk, has brought out the Great Suffolk Nature Survey, which quizzes participants on the county's "struggling" wildlife.

It asks about their experiences with local wildlife, how they get involved with local nature, and their attitudes towards conservation, climate change and environmental projects.

The short survey comes weeks after a devastating wildfire at Dunwich Heath and nearby RSPB Minsmere destroyed vital wildlife habitats, which could take years to recover.

Jack Cripps, head of marketing and communications at SWT, said: "The county's landscapes and wildlife are a huge part of what I and so many others who live here are proud of.

"But our wildlife is struggling and we're really starting to feel the impacts of our changing climate. This survey will go a bit deeper into what local people think and feel about nature.

"Everyone can get involved with protecting nature, and the results of the survey will guide Suffolk Wildlife Trust's future community projects and campaigning."

This is the first time SWT has run its own survey, although it has previously gathered local responses as part of the nationwide The Great Big Nature Survey.

Hannah Page, from the University of Suffolk, said it was "delighted" to be supporting the trust with the "important project".

She also said there would be an opportunity for a student from the university to help roll out the survey thanks to a paid student placement from the county council.

Hannah Page, from the University of Suffolk, said it was "delighted" to be supporting the trust with the "important project".
She also said there would be an opportunity for a student from the university to help roll out the survey thanks to a paid student placement from the county council.

articles.title: Inspectors to assess police following Henry Nowak murder
articles.summary: Hampshire Police officers initially arrested the student and placed him in handcuffs as he lay dying.
articles.body:
An inspection into how a police force responds to violent incidents has been launched in the wake of Henry Nowak's murder.

The 18-year-old student was stabbed in Southampton by Vickrum Digwa , who lied to police and insisted he had been the victim of a racist attack.

Hampshire Police officers initially arrested Nowak and placed him in handcuffs as he lay dying.

His Majesty's Inspectorate of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue Service (HMICFRS) will assess the force's processes, training and how officers are supported to make sound and impartial judgements.

The inspection was requested by Hampshire Police and Crime Commissioner Donna Jones, who said the public "must have confidence" in the force.

"This inspection will provide an independent assessment of the force's training, processes and culture, including the handling of allegations of racially aggravated assault," she said.

"Henry's family deserve answers, and the public deserve reassurance that their police service is equipped to recognise victims and provide the highest standard of care when it matters most."

Nowak, from Chafford Hundred in Essex, was a first-year student at the University of Southampton at the time of his death.

Digwa was jailed for life in June with a minimum term of 21 years, after the judge rejected his claims of self-defence.

Previously released video of Nowak in handcuffs caused national outrage and sparked violent disorder in Southampton.

The case has since led to national debates over policing, race and knife laws.

Inspectors will assess the end-to-end process of a police response through the control room, including call handling, dispatch and initial attendance at incidents of serious violence.

It will also examine decision-making and risk assessment training, focussing on how officers are helped to make bias-free decisions and identify where immediate action like first aid is required.

More stories from Hampshire & the Isle of Wight

Listen to the latest news from Hampshire and the Isle of Wight

Jones said: "The public must have confidence that police officers receive the right information, the right training and the right support to make critical decisions."

The inspection will not examine the conduct or actions of officers who responded to the 3 December incident involving Nowak, which is subject to a separate investigation by the Independent Office for Police Conduct.

The Commissioner's office said the scope of the review had been carefully designed to avoid interfering with other judicial or conduct processes.

articles.title: Balen gets medical pass to wear trademark dark glasses in parliament
articles.summary: South Asia News: Nepal parliament secretariat cleared PM Balendra Shah to wear his trademark dark sunglasses inside parliament on medical grounds after his office subm.
articles.body: Nepal parliament secretariat cleared PM Balendra Shah to wear his trademark dark sunglasses inside parliament on medical grounds after his office submitted a medical report, ending a row over whether such eyewear belonged in the House. Speaker Dol Prasad Aryal had earlier advised lawmakers against wearing dark glasses in the chamber following public criticism.Parliament secretariat spokesperson Ekaram Giri said Shahâs office submitted documents showing he needed them for medical reasons -- his doctor advised him to wear the shades because he had "discomfort seeing in bright light". Shah is scheduled to face lawmakers in a direct question-and-answer session on Wednesday, amid opposition criticism over his repeated absence from parliament.Shahâs rectangular black shades had long been part of his public image, accompanying the former rapper and Kathmandu mayor through his rise to Nepalâs top office. Ahead of Nepalâs March 5 elections, supporters dubbed the look âBalen dai ko chashmaâ, triggering a fashion craze among young voters. Similar black rectangular frames sold out at several Kathmandu shops and online stores as demand surged, with retailers marketing lookalikes. Often paired with his all-black outfits, the shades became one of the most recognisable symbols of Shahâs youth appeal.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Teaching kids about money: What's the right age to start?
articles.summary: Teaching kids about money starts at home — and beginning early is key. Here's why, along with some age-appropriate lessons you can try.
articles.body:
Some offers on this page are from advertisers who pay us, which may affect which products we write about, but not our recommendations. See our Advertiser Disclosure .

When it comes to teaching your kids about money, it's never too early to start. Of course, their age will determine how detailed and complex those lessons should be.

Here's why you should start having conversations about money with your kids right away, and how to frame those discussions according to their age.

The benefits of teaching kids about money early

According to a recent survey by U.S. Bank and Morning Consult, about two-thirds of parents say they have already started or plan to start teaching basic money management concepts before their children turn 12.

"Today's parents are the first generation where a majority are choosing to have open conversations with their kids about money — and at an early age," said Arijit Roy, head of consumer and business banking products at U.S. Bank, in a statement.

For example, the survey found 62% of Gen Z respondents had these types of money conversations growing up, compared to less than half (49%) of baby boomers.

Studies have found that introducing the concept of money management early can help your child gain the knowledge and confidence to make more informed financial decisions later in life, as well as build more positive financial habits.

In fact, 39 states now require personal finance courses for high school graduation. And a Federal Reserve Bank of New York study found that those who received mandatory financial education in high school were more likely to make sound financial decisions as adults than those who didn't receive any education.

However, experts say it's important for parents to start these conversations at home and not leave the responsibility solely up to schools.

"Kids start forming an understanding of money and begin developing their own money habits far earlier than parents might realize," said Alaina Trivax, author of Follow the Money and founder of financial literacy platform Let's Make It Grow . "We already teach our kids values like kindness and respect, and about how to ride a bike and brush their teeth. Financial literacy skills belong on that same list."

What are some age-appropriate money lessons?

Helping your child learn about money doesn't necessarily mean sitting them down and conducting an official lesson. There are teachable moments in everyday life that parents can use as an opportunity to talk about money. And children as young as preschool age can grasp many of these concepts.

For example, in their younger years, you can start by explaining why parents go to work, how money is earned, and how that money helps the family afford everyday expenses. These initial conversations can then lead to further questions and discussions about budgeting, borrowing, investing, and more.

Parents can also involve young children in meal planning and grocery shopping, cluing them in to how money plays a role in their home and everyday life.

Trivax noted that children ages 8 to 11 are usually ready for more independence, which could involve earning a little money and deciding how to budget it. "Take them grocery shopping with you for a few easy lessons. Try handing them a name-brand and a store-brand cereal box, and point out their different prices," Trivax explained. "Ask your child why one might cost more, and if the difference seems worth it."

By middle school, Trivax added, kids can handle more complex concepts, such as opportunity cost. For example, spending $60 on a video game today might mean saying no to a concert ticket next month, she said. "As they head into high school and college, they'll need to know how to budget, save, and invest their money too."

The road to smart financial decisions starts at home. Parents have the opportunity to use everyday errands, purchases, and money choices as lessons that can shape a child's financial future — and they don't have to wait until their child can count coins and bills to start.

The earlier these conversations begin, the more time there is to build strong habits and decision-making skills that can serve as a foundation for a better financial future.

articles.title: In 1973, Dr Martin Cooper made world's first mobile phone call to his rival at Bell Labs; but all he heard back was silence as ...
articles.summary: Tech News News: âOn April 3, 1973, Motorola engineer Dr Martin Cooper made what is widely recognised as the first mobile phone call. Standing on a New York City stree.
articles.body: âOn April 3, 1973, Motorola engineer Dr Martin Cooper made what is widely recognised as the first mobile phone call. Standing on a New York City street, Cooper called Joel Engel, an engineer at Bell Laboratories and his rival in the race to develop mobile communications. Cooper told Engel he was calling from a âpersonal, handheld portable cell phone,â but all he heard back was silence as he presumed his competitor had been left speechless.âThe call came as Motorola and Bell Laboratories were pursuing different approaches to mobile communications. Bell Labs was working on car-based phones, while Cooper and Motorola were developing a device a person could carry. By making the call in the middle of a street rather than from a vehicle, Cooper demonstrated the idea of a truly portable mobile phone.âThe history of the first mobile phone callâIn the 1970s, Bell Laboratories was developing mobile phones designed for use inside cars. Motorola was pursuing a different approach that would allow people to carry their phones with them.âCooper's 1973 call was made using an early prototype that would eventually lead to the Motorola DynaTAC 8000X. The first mobile phone sold to consumers did not arrive until 1984, more than a decade after Cooper made his call.âThe DynaTAC 8000X was considerably different from the phones people use today. It could provide around 30 minutes of talk time, required about 10 hours to recharge and weighed roughly 1.7 pounds. Its price was also high, equivalent to about $11,700 in today's money.âThe 1973 demonstration was therefore not a consumer product launch. It showed that a mobile phone could operate independently of a vehicle and be carried by an individual.âWhy Martin Cooper called his Bell Labs rivalâCooper later explained that the call had a broader purpose beyond the competition between Motorola and Bell Labs. In a 2013 BGR interview marking the 40th anniversary of the call, he said his goal was to prevent AT&T, which owned Bell Laboratories at the time, from âcreating a monopoly in the cell phones. And not only that, but a monopoly in car telephones.ââCooper acknowledged that AT&T had invented cellular technology in 1947, but said Motorola did not want the company to become the sole provider once mobile phones reached consumers. âWe thought the world was ready for the freedom you get in having personal communications. And we sure didn't want to get put out of business.ââThe rivalry between the two companies was therefore connected to how mobile communications would develop and who would control the emerging market.âCooper later acknowledged that the call also had a competitive element. In 2023, he told NPR that he was ânot averse to rubbing [Engel's] nose in our achievement.ââThe exchange took place when mobile communications were still largely experimental. The phone Cooper used was bulky by modern standards and had limited battery life, but the call demonstrated that a person could make a wireless call without being connected to a vehicle.âMore than five decades later, mobile phones have evolved from large devices designed primarily for voice calls into computers used for messaging, photography, navigation, internet access and other functions. Cooper's 1973 call to Engel marked an early step in that transition.Get the latest technology news and updates. Download the TOI App.
