articles.title: Ukrainians seeking beauty in a bomb-scarred city
articles.summary: The Ukrainian city of Izyum has been splintered by Russian bombs -- but 21-year-old Violetta Dezhyna's job is to find beauty in those broken places and help...
articles.body:
The Ukrainian city of Izyum has been splintered by Russian bombs -- but 21-year-old Violetta Dezhyna's job is to find beauty in those broken places and help keep the city alive, even as Russia advances once more.

In dusty streets teeming with men in camouflage and scattered with wrecked military vehicles she scours for scenes of normality to post on the city social media pages.

Pruned flowerbeds stand in front of gutted and mangled apartment blocks.

"Here the buildings are destroyed, not pretty. Here, it seems, there's a fountain, but on the other side there's a ruined building," said Dezhyna, who works for the local admimistration.

"I try to find angles where those things aren't visible."

Russia's army captured Izyum, the gateway to Ukraine's eastern Donbas region -- a key target for Russian President Vladimir Putin -- at the start of its 2022 invasion, occupying it for six months before Ukraine retook control.

The majority of Izyum's pre-invasion population of 45,000 came back after Russian troops were pushed back some 60 kilometres (36 miles) in a lightning Ukrainian counter-offensive in autumn 2022.

Dezhyna, then a teenager, returned with her family to help "rebuild" the wounded city.

But the battles have left deep scars on Izyum and its residents -- both physical and psychological.

Months of grinding advances have brought the Russian troops to within 30 kilometres (18 miles) of Izyum again.

And Dezhyna is watching many of her young friends leave once more.

To be around people and feel a sense of community, she frequents the local gym.

Hidden in the basement of a supermarket, the thick smell of sweat hangs heavy in the air as she pushes weights alongside bearded muscle-men.

In between sets, she chats casually with soldiers and their wives -- many more than twice her age.

Over the echo of nearby explosions, they sometimes play beach volleyball near the river -- "the most beautiful place in town".

Back in the office, cracks in the walls and aluminium tape over the windows -- to stop glass shards flying into the building in case of an explosion -- reveal the constant danger faced by those in the city.

Another worker -- also a young women, with blue hair -- took out a small mirror, applied lip gloss then lifted her eyes to the window: taking in the sight of anti-drone nets that engulf the city's buildings and roads.

In another official building across town, violin notes mixed with air raid sirens.

Tamara Georgina, 58, was preparing the room for an upcoming wedding.

"This is resistance ... to spite the enemy. We work, we live, we show that we're not surrendering. This is our town and we're rebuilding it," she told AFP.

Behind her the groom, a soldier, quickly answered his phone.

Residents say many buildings in the city are "marked" -- a term meaning they are a known target for the Russian army.

They include many places where young people typically gather, like the city's Palace of Culture.

Some still kill time in the ruins of what was once a city landmark -- vaping amid the smell of urine.

Dezhyna, who leaves a faint floral scent behind her as she paces the streets, is lobbying officials to rebuild a skate park.

If young people leave, "there will be no future at all," she said.

"I want our community to thrive. I don't want it to remain ... grey."

Roughly 2,000 children still live in Izyum.

School activities -- transformed by the war into classes such as "emotional resilience" -- take place in the building's basement.

Classes for Dezhyna -- then in her final year -- were cancelled on February 24, 2022, the day Russia invaded.

Her prom dress was supposed to arrive the next day.

"I can't say the feelings are very good," she said, walking through her old classroom, chairs now covered in dust.

Russian troops had used it as a base during their occupation of the city.

With them inching closer to the city, Dezhyna and her parents are again thinking about whether they should flee to refuge, far from her beloved Izyum.

"We have to think about it, but I don't want to," she said.

With them inching closer to the city, Dezhyna and her parents are again thinking about whether they should flee to refuge, far from her beloved Izyum.
"We have to think about it, but I don't want to," she said.

articles.title: Iran, Oman Push Talks for ‘Interim’ Reopening of Hormuz Strait
articles.summary: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and his Omani counterpart Badr Albusaidi discussed an “interim framework” aimed at resuming shipping through the Stra...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and his Omani counterpart Badr Albusaidi discussed an "interim framework" aimed at resuming shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, according to a joint statement carried by the Oman News Agency, as the two sides press ahead with long-running talks over navigation through the key waterway.

Lutnick's Intervention in Canada Talks Draws Praise, Blame

Apple Gears Up to Launch Its First New Mac Mini in Two Years

Bessent's Mentor Druckenmiller Calls Bond Buying a Mistake

Canadians Brace for Economic Pain as 50% US Tariffs Take Effect

Canada Sees Long Trade War With US That May Last Beyond Midterms

The initiative seeks to establish a "temporary joint maritime corridor" and project for mine clearance to restore safe navigation through the area, according to the statement.

Technical talks between the two sides will continue with the aim of agreeing on a permanent maritime corridor, the future administration of the strait, as well as a mechanism for information exchange, traffic management, and the provision of relevant maritime and security services, it said.

The Strait of Hormuz, through which about a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas previously passed, has remained largely closed since March, when Iran moved to block the waterway following US and Israeli attacks on Feb. 28 that killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei.

Earlier Tuesday, US President Donald Trump said the US Navy had cleared mines from the strait, in a move aimed at opening shipping flows through the vital waterway. The social media announcement came a day after the US announced a raft of new economic sanctions designed to deter economic and financial partnerships with the country and ratchet up pressure on Tehran.

"Iran has been notified that any ship or boat placing new mines will be immediately and systematically destroyed," Trump said.

Trump provided no evidence for his assertion that the strait was cleared of mines, something he has claimed before. European officials have expressed skepticism in the past, given the time-consuming and complicated nature of mine clearing.

Tehran had previously stated that it is focusing solely on talks with Oman as the other littoral state of the Strait of Hormuz, maintaining that those discussions are independent of stalled negotiations with Washington.

But there were indications Tuesday that the negotiations could incorporate other nations in the region. The joint statement from Iran and Oman said that both sides "emphasized the importance of holding joint talks with regional countries bordering the waters of the Persian Gulf" as the months-long discussions continue. And Albusaidi, in a social media post, said that discussions with regional partners "will be conducted in support of peace and cooperation, stability and freedom of navigation."

articles.title: Creator ties AI data centers to water crisis, offers state-by-state legal safeguards
articles.summary: "What most people don't know is that access to water and a healthful environment is a right!"
articles.body:
An Instagram creator's recent reel explained that water scarcity is not only about dwindling resources.

The creator urged viewers to learn what legal safeguards exist in their states as AI and data centers place mounting strain on water supplies.

In a post shared on Aug. 19, Instagram creator Ayana Gray (@ayana.g123) addressed the growing tension between public water supplies and the AI data center boom.

Gray linked shrinking water supplies to several pressures, including "increased heat, general human industrial activity, and of course, data centers and AI."

"The water crisis is already happening, and this is just the beginning," she warned.

Data centers support everything from chatbots to cloud storage, but they require large amounts of electricity and their cooling systems often depend on significant water use, especially in hot or drought-prone regions.

Rather than focusing solely on expansion and permitting, the post emphasized legal rights related to environmental conditions.

"What most people don't know is that access to water and a healthful environment is a right! It's a right we must protect," Gray wrote.

The poster also asked followers to name their states in the comments so she could respond with information about local laws.

"For more information on your state's position on the right to a healthful environment, respond with the name of your state and I will reply to you about your state's laws!" she said.

Concern over AI's environmental footprint goes beyond water alone.

These tools run on energy-intensive chips housed in data centers, placing new demand on the power grid, which is already being asked to handle rising cooling demand, electric vehicles , and industrial expansion.

AI can help utilities balance electricity demand, improve building efficiency, accelerate clean energy planning, and support more accurate forecasting for solar and wind.

However, those potential benefits exist alongside real risks, including high electricity and cooling needs, cybersecurity concerns, misuse, and higher utility costs if infrastructure expands faster than cleaner power supplies do.

When large industrial users move into a community, residents often worry about whether local water supplies will remain dependable during hotter, drier periods and whether the burdens and benefits are being shared fairly.

States vary widely in how they approach environmental rights, water protections, and industrial permitting.

Gray's invitation for people to comment with their state names exposed a worrisome truth: Many people do not know what legal protections exist where they live.

Public hearings, water-use plans, energy-sourcing disclosures, and utility filings can reveal whether a project is expected to rely heavily on local water supplies or strain the grid.

Policymakers and utilities can require greater transparency around how AI infrastructure uses power and water.

Stronger reporting, more efficient cooling systems, cleaner electricity procurement, and better planning can help reduce some of the pressure these facilities place on communities.

articles.title: Calls for GPS monitoring of domestic abuse suspects after murder of Stacy Hunter
articles.summary: An online petition calls for greater use of technology to protect women from abusive partners following the killing of Stacy Hunter in Renfrewshire.
articles.body:
Domestic abuse campaigners are calling for greater use of location tracking technology to monitor high-risk suspects following the murder of a woman in Renfrewshire last month.

An online petition is calling for a "Stacy's law" in memory of Stacy Hunter who was killed at her home near Houston by her estranged husband while he was on bail.

Scottish ministers have previously faced criticism over the slow rollout of Global Positioning System (GPS) equipment, which is used far less in Scotland than in some other countries.

The Scottish government said it was listening to victims and support organisations and would carefully consider the petition.

Woman found dead was murdered, police say, as man's death still 'unexplained'

Man found dead with murdered wife had been accused of attacking her

The campaign has been started by Lynne Mackenzie, herself a domestic abuse survivor, who lives a few miles from the isolated cottage where Stacy was killed in July.

Stacy's husband Jim Mair, 43, whose body was found beside her, had been charged with assaulting her but had reportedly been granted bail on condition that he did not approach her.

While Mackenzie did not know Stacy personally, she said she was shocked at her murder which happened just six days after the death of another domestic abuse victim, Vikki Soloman, in Edinburgh.

She told BBC Scotland News the killings led her to question whether enough was being done to protect women in Stacy's situation.

"Every time driving in and out of the village I was aware of the police at the end of the road," she said.

"And it really got me thinking what could we have done? What could have been put in place beforehand? What else do we need?"

She has been in contact with Stacy's family who have agreed for her name to be associated with the campaign.

The petition calls for high-risk domestic abuse perpetrators or suspects released on bail to have their location monitored using GPS equipment.

This could include individually assessed exclusion zones around victim's homes or workplaces and alerts that trigger police responses when conditions are breached.

Mike Nellis, emeritus professor of criminal and community justice at the University of Strathclyde and one of the UK's leading experts on electronic monitoring, said it was perfectly feasible to introduce such a system.

He said it could work by setting an exclusion zone around a victim's home that triggered an alert if an abuser violated it, although the zone would have to be sufficiently large to allow time for police to get there first.

Prof Nellis said that while Scotland has been slow to embrace GPS technology, the campaign could now find itself "pushing at an open door" because ministers are actively exploring ways of reducing the prison population.

However, he cautioned that no system was foolproof.

"I think probably every jurisdiction that has used it has at one point in time had an offender who still managed to assault, injure or kill the victim," he told BBC Scotland News.

"It's a helpful solution but it's not perfect."

He also added that some women's support groups have in the past voiced concern that such systems might give a false sense of security.

In Scotland, electronic tagging has mainly relied on older radio frequency (RF) equipment which is focused on home curfews or detention.

These devices are linked to a receiver in the offender's home and cannot track movements away from the property.

Last year, the independent public body Community Justice Scotland (CJS) issued an urgent National Improvement Recommendation to the Scottish government urging it to accelerate the expansion of more sophisticated monitoring systems.

CJS expressed frustration that neither GPS nor alcohol monitoring technologies had been adopted in Scotland despite an expert group having backed them in 2016.

By contrast, both technologies have already been widely used in England and Wales since 2018 and there are plans to start imposing new restriction zones on offenders this autumn.

Scotland's victims minister, Kirsten Oswald, said her thoughts were with Stacy's family.

In a statement she said: "We are listening carefully to victims and support organisations about what more can be done to prevent and tackle violence against women and girls and we will carefully consider the petition.

"The first minister has pledged his personal leadership on tackling the scourge of violence against women and girls.

"As the first minister has made clear, government has a vital role to play in tackling violence against women and girls, but lasting change requires all of us to play our part."

She added: "Men, in particular, must challenge sexism, confront abusive behaviour and help create a culture where every woman and girl can live free from violence, abuse and fear.

"While decisions on bail and remand are always a matter for the independent court, bail can be electronically monitored."

Lynne Mackenzie is a co-founder of Rise Against Abuse , a not-for-profit group which supports those affected by domestic abuse, but she has started the petition in an individual capacity.

Stacy's family now prefer her to be remembered by her pre-marriage surname Hunter, rather than her husband's name Mair.

Man charged with murdering ex-partner found dead in jail

articles.title: India snake rescue turns fatal after cobra escapes broken box and bites handler
articles.summary: Human settlement, land-use changes, and daily activity can increase encounters with wild animals.
articles.body:
A snake rescue in central India ended in tragedy after 25-year-old snake rescuer Aman Gohiya died from a cobra bite after capturing the animal.

In Dungra village in Mandla district, a cobra bite during a rescue call later proved fatal for Gohiya, according to Bhaskar English .

Gohiya and a companion went to a village 6 kilometers (about 3.7 miles) away from Bichhiya to remove the snake.

The snake rescuer captured the cobra, but the bite occurred afterward. When Gohiya attempted to place the captured snake into a plastic box, it escaped through a damaged section at the back and bit his leg, the outlet reported.

After being taken first to the Bichhiya Community Health Centre, Gohiya was referred to Mandla District Hospital. Mandla District Hospital Civil Surgeon Dr. Vijay Dhurve said MD Medicine specialist Dr. Mohsin supervised his treatment there, but his condition remained critical despite medical care.

Bhaskar English reported that Gohiya attempted to contain the snake, holding the cobra with one hand and the container with the other. The container was reportedly broken, and Gohiya was not wearing protective clothing.

Snake rescues like this often happen in villages and expanding residential areas, where people and wildlife are pushed into closer contact.

When snakes enter homes, farms, or storage spaces, residents may call local rescuers in hopes of preventing harm to both people and the animal.

Human settlement, land-use changes, and daily activity can increase encounters with wild animals. Attacks are often shaped by the ways humans alter habitats and come into closer range of wildlife.

articles.title: US starts returning staff to Middle East missions after Iran war evacuations, sources say
articles.summary: By Humeyra Pamuk WASHINGTON, Aug 25 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump's administration is starting to send personnel back to some diplomatic missions in the...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, Aug 25 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump's administration is starting to send personnel back to some diplomatic missions in the Middle East that were evacuated ‌or downsized amid tensions with Iran, two people familiar with the matter told Reuters.

The ‌posts in Lebanon, Israel, Saudi Arabia and Baghdad, Iraq, are among those where staff will return, the sources said. Family ​members will also be allowed to return to the U.S. post in Riyadh, they added.

The move suggests Washington sees a lower risk of the conflict with Iran escalating in the near term, though some embassies will initially operate below full capacity.

Some embassies will initially operate at no more than 85% ‌of authorized personnel levels, the sources ⁠said.

The return of some staff is expected to start as early as this week, one of the sources said.

The United States pulled out staff from ⁠embassies across the Middle East after joint U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran began on February 28. Some embassies in Gulf Arab countries such as Saudi Arabia and Kuwait came under fire from Iran, forcing the latter ​to ​temporarily close.

Since then, heavy fighting has subsided even though ​a U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports ‌persists and the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for oil and commodities shipping, remains shut with diplomatic efforts to end the war stalled.

A U.S. State Department spokesperson told Reuters in an emailed statement that the department continuously reviews the security posture of its diplomatic missions worldwide.

"Based on our latest assessment, we are adjusting our staffing posture at certain posts in the Middle East ‌to ensure we can continue advancing U.S. foreign policy ​objectives while protecting the safety and security of our personnel," ​the spokesperson said.

The New York Times earlier ​reported the return of diplomats and the easing of emergency measures and ‌said embassies in Jordan, Oman, Kuwait and ​Qatar were also expected to ​restore higher personnel levels, citing an internal document.

U.S. embassies in Israel, Jordan and Oman would ultimately return to full staffing, while missions in the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, ​Qatar and Lebanon would initially ‌be capped at 85% staffing. Posts in Iraq, Kuwait and Bahrain would be limited ​to 75%, the newspaper added.

(Reporting by Humeyra Pamuk Additional reporting by Bipasha Dey and ​Abu Sultan in Bengaluru Editing by Sanjeev Miglani)

articles.title: Texas nature center rebuilt after Guadalupe flood, but Town Creek flood wrecked the interior again
articles.summary: "All of the new renovations from 2025 were damaged."
articles.body:
Rebuilding after one flood is difficult enough. At Texas' Riverside Nature Center, staff restored the historic Lawson Store after a 2025 flood linked to backflow from the Guadalupe River, only to see a 2026 flood rip through the interior all over again.

The Kerr County Lead reported that the floods were very different, according to Riverside Nature Center's executive director Becky Etzler. The 2025 event followed the more familiar pattern of Guadalupe River backflow, but the 2026 flooding came out of Town Creek, which she described as a "rampaging monster."

Although the structure remained intact, the interior work completed after the first disaster did not. "All of the new renovations from 2025 were damaged," Etzler said. "We had to virtually start again in the Lawson Store."

Riverside Nature Center began in 1994 under founder Susan Sander, a Wisconsin-born freelance photographer. Through volunteer effort and privately raised funds, the organization acquired three historic homesteads and developed them into a regional natural resource hub.

Staff naturalist China Rubiano now oversees surveys of birds, butterflies, and plants, monitors seasonal changes in native species, and cares for Shucks — the center's captive-bred corn snake.

A large shipping container being used for storage after the first flood broke loose from its foundation, drifted across the parking lot, and crashed into the children's music garden, damaging several instruments.

Yet when it came to a stop, the container was positioned to shield the center's new 20,000-gallon rainwater-harvesting tank, which The Kerr County Lead reported was miraculously left undamaged.

When floodwaters damage community spaces, they can interrupt children's programs, create public health concerns through contaminated water and debris, strain local budgets with repeated repairs, and destabilize organizations families rely on for education and safe gathering spaces.

Rebuilding once is expensive, but rebuilding twice can drain time, money, and momentum from nonprofits, workers, and communities already struggling to recover.

Despite repeated damage, Riverside Nature Center has kept its programs going. According to The Kerr County Lead , Sprouts preschool nature classes grew from five families to more than 30 children, and Riverside Rangers and Wildflower Bunch seed-collection walks are still happening.

The center is adding help as it rebuilds. Former Schreiner University intern Bryley Torres joined the staff as the membership and marketing coordinator to support outreach efforts. Looking further ahead, Etzler hopes to expand the visitor center, continue building out the Nature Lab, and one day open an outdoor nature school.

The center is also maintaining its education schedule. A free talk was held on Aug. 19 with Kerr County AgriLife Extension Agent Sam Womble to discuss the New World screwworm and its risks to livestock, ranching, and pets.

Yet when it came to a stop, the container was positioned to shield the center's new 20,000-gallon rainwater-harvesting tank, which The Kerr County Lead reported was miraculously left undamaged.

When floodwaters damage community spaces, they can interrupt children's programs, create public health concerns through contaminated water and debris, strain local budgets with repeated repairs, and destabilize organizations families rely on for education and safe gathering spaces.
Rebuilding once is expensive, but rebuilding twice can drain time, money, and momentum from nonprofits, workers, and communities already struggling to recover.

Despite repeated damage, Riverside Nature Center has kept its programs going. According to The Kerr County Lead , Sprouts preschool nature classes grew from five families to more than 30 children, and Riverside Rangers and Wildflower Bunch seed-collection walks are still happening.

The center is adding help as it rebuilds. Former Schreiner University intern Bryley Torres joined the staff as the membership and marketing coordinator to support outreach efforts. Looking further ahead, Etzler hopes to expand the visitor center, continue building out the Nature Lab, and one day open an outdoor nature school.

The center is also maintaining its education schedule. A free talk was held on Aug. 19 with Kerr County AgriLife Extension Agent Sam Womble to discuss the New World screwworm and its risks to livestock, ranching, and pets.

articles.title: Bulls Legend Reveals What It Will Take To Return To Glory
articles.summary: The Chicago Bulls finally feel like they’re moving in the right direction after embracing a full-scale rebuild over the past 12 months.However, part of being...
articles.body:
The Chicago Bulls finally feel like they're moving in the right direction after embracing a full-scale rebuild over the past 12 months.

However, part of being a rebuilding team is remaining patient as the young talent on the roster develops and finds their roles in the league. Of course, that sounds easy in practice, but the process can take multiple years, and sometimes, teams get impatient.

During a recent conversation with Kyle Odegard of Action Network, former Bulls champion Horace Grant urged the team to remain patient with the franchise's new young core.

"To go back iconic like we did back in the day, it's going to take some work," Grant said. "It's going to take some patience. But with the core they have now, staying healthy, and then I still think they need a little bit more leadership in that locker room. I played with some great leaders in Chicago. MJ, Pip, Bill Cartwright, you can throw John Paxson in there as well."

"The city is going to have to stay patient, because they are a very young crew," Grant said. "I tell people this: when Scottie and I first got there in '87, we were getting our heads knocked in by the Detroit Pistons almost every year. It took patience. It took trust in each other, and then the rest is history."

Chicago's new young core has the potential to take the team back toward the top of the Eastern Conference. However, the path isn't going to be easy, and moves will need to be made along the way. Still, right now, the fanbase will undoubtedly be excited about what's to come.

Grant Shares Thoughts on Bulls' Caleb Wilson

During his conversation with Action Network, Grant also shared his thoughts on Caleb Wilson, who the Bulls selected with the fourth-overall pick in the 2026 NBA Draft.

"Oh my goodness, man," Grant said. "What a beast. What a freakin' beast. He has all the intangibles, the skill set. But what I love about him is that he has the mindset of a killer. A dog. He goes out and gets it."

Granted continued, noting how Wilson is one of Chicago's best draft picks since the addition of Derrick Rose .

"It's one of the best draft picks since Derrick Rose. I'm not going to put him with MJ and myself and Pip, but since Derrick Rose, one of the greatest choices the Bulls have made, in my humble opinion."

Wilson undoubtedly has superstar potential. However, he'll need to navigate his rookie season and continue improving long-term in order to reach his ceiling.

Bulls Have Solid Coach In Tiago Splitter

Grant also noted that his nephew, Jerami Grant , was impressed by new Bulls head coach, Tiago Splitter last season.

"I haven't talked to (Splitter) as of yet," Grant said. "I'm pretty sure he's still trying to get pieces around him, as far as assistant coaches, player development guys. But the craziest thing is he coached my nephew down in Portland."

Chicago is well position to develop into a genuine force in the coming years. However, in order for that to happen, everyone needs to be on the same page and remain patient.

articles.title: Cincinnati Reds vs. San Francisco Giants – Brady Singer vs. Adrian Houser
articles.summary: Another night of the Cincinnati Reds attempting to play the game of baseball professionally.
articles.body:
The Cincinnati Reds failed to score so much as a single run in Monday's series opener against the San Francisco Giants in the heavy air of northern California, losing 5-0 on a night where Chase Burns simply didn't have it for one of the very few times we've seen such a thing in his big league career.

On Tuesday, they'll send struggling starter Brady Singer to the mound to try to rectify things. I'd be far more optimistic about that concept if they weren't also sending out a lineup that features Hector Rodriguez, Ke'Bryan Hayes, and TJ Friedl in it (hitting back to back to back), but here we are regardless.

It's once again a late-night start, so you'll have to pry your eyes open with toothpicks to stay up and indulge in all of the scintillating action between these two going-nowhere rosters.

First pitch is slated to be chucked by Houser at 9:45 PM ET.

Here's how both clubs will line up to start:

articles.title: Seahawks waive UDFA RB Anthony Hankerson
articles.summary: The Seahawks move on from Hankerson following the team’s second preseason matchup against the Titans.
articles.body:
The Seattle Seahawks waived running back Anthony Hankerson on Monday, according to ESPN's Brady Henderson, prior to their final preseason matchup against the Kansas City Chiefs on Friday.

Hankerson rushed for 1,086 yards in 2025 at Oregon State prior to entering the NFL as an undrafted free agent with the Miami Dolphins in May. He was waived by the Dolphins in August, before signing with the Seahawks during training camp.

The 22-year-old Hankerson rushed for 10 yards on five carries, and added nine receiving yards in the Seahawks' 19-16 loss to the Tennessee Titans in Week 2 of the preseason prior to being waived by Seattle.

The Seahawks move forward with a running back unit consisting of Jadarian Price, Zach Charbonnet , George Holani , Emanuel Wilson , Velus Jones Jr., and Jacardia Wright. Hankerson will be able to sign with another team as a free agent if he is not claimed off of waivers.

articles.title: 10 observations from Eagles’ open training camp practice at the Linc
articles.summary: Riq Woolen’s two interceptions, DeVonta Smith’s return and creative formations highlighted the Eagles’ open practice at the Linc
articles.body:
Philadelphia always supports the Eagles Autism Foundation , and the festivities continued on Tuesday as more than 45,000 fans attended the annual open practice at Lincoln Financial Field. They were treated to several explosive offensive plays, two defensive touchdowns and another competitive training camp session.

Riq Woolen produced the biggest performance of the night, while DeVonta Smith showed why his return changes the outlook for Philadelphia 's offense. Jalen Hurts experienced some encouraging moments and costly mistakes during an uneven performance.

Here are 10 observations from Tuesday's practice.

Woolen's status as a starting cornerback has never been in question, and Tuesday demonstrated why Philadelphia signed him to a one-year, $15 million contract. Woolen intercepted Hurts twice. He undercut a dig route intended for Makai Lemon on the first takeaway, then jumped an out route to Smith during a two-minute drill and returned it for a touchdown.

His length, closing speed and ability to recognize route concepts give Philadelphia another potential playmaker opposite Quinyon Mitchell .

2. Jalen Hurts delivered an uneven performance

Hurts generated several touchdowns and explosive completions, but his two interceptions prevented the performance from being considered a successful one. The first turnover came on a late throw over the middle. Hurts threw the second interception off his back foot while facing pressure from Jalyx Hunt . Woolen anticipated the out route and finished the play in the end zone.

Hurts also underthrew Smith on a deep post that could have resulted in a touchdown.

3. DeVonta Smith looked healthy and explosive

Smith caught passes on a deep out and a play-action rollout during the first move-the-ball period. He later wrestled away a deep crossing route against tight coverage from Mitchell and accelerated toward the end zone. Smith also adjusted his angle on a dig route when Woolen attempted to undercut it. The route prevented Woolen from producing another takeaway and allowed Smith to turn upfield for a potential touchdown.

There were imperfections, including a drop on a third-down crossing route, but Smith's movement and explosiveness were encouraging.

4. Sean Mannion continued showing creativity

Philadelphia used Lemon out of the backfield during a red-zone period. The rookie ran a wheel route along the left sideline and was left uncovered for a touchdown. Dallas Goedert also aligned as an offset H-back, another indication that Mannion plans to use multiple players in fullback-style roles. The Eagles do not have to carry a traditional fullback if Goedert, Barkley, Lemon and other skill players can execute those responsibilities through formations and motion.

5. Jalyx Hunt created consistent pressure

Hunt overwhelmed Fred Johnson after Lane Johnson left practice and Markel Bell was unavailable. His pressure also contributed to Hurts' second interception. The third-year edge rusher has spent the summer establishing himself as a legitimate starter. Tuesday offered more evidence that his combination of length, speed and developing pass-rush technique can become a problem for opposing tackles.

6. Philadelphia's offensive line depth was tested

Landon Dickerson received a scheduled rest night, allowing Drew Kendall to work at first-team left guard. Lane Johnson walked off with a trainer and remained on the sideline for the remainder of the competitive periods. Fred Johnson replaced him at right tackle and surrendered consecutive pressures during one series. With Bell sidelined by thumb and leg injuries, Philadelphia was forced to reach further into its offensive tackle depth. That move provided the clearest reminder of why reserve offensive line jobs are so important.

7. Makai Lemon's role continues expanding

Lemon's most impressive moment came when he aligned at running back and caught an uncontested wheel-route touchdown. The formation displayed how Mannion can manufacture favorable matchups for the first-round pick.

The rookie was also the intended receiver on Woolen's first interception, providing another example of the timing Lemon and Hurts must continue developing after the receiver missed significant practice time with a hamstring injury. The Eagles are finding different ways to get the football into Lemon's hands. That may matter more than assigning him to a single traditional receiver position.

8. Saquon Barkley remains a matchup problem

Barkley juked Baun during the first move-the-ball period and broke into the open field for a substantial gain.

His best receiving play came in the red zone when Hurts placed a wheel-route touchdown over Barkley's outside shoulder. Baun had strong coverage, but the placement and catch were too precise to defend. Philadelphia has continued looking for ways to feature Barkley as a receiver in Mannion's offense.

9. The defensive backfield challenged every throw

Mitchell broke up the underthrown deep pass intended for Smith. Jihaad Campbell disrupted a throw to Lemon, while Woolen produced the two interceptions.

Philadelphia's offense created explosive plays, but the defense consistently challenged receivers and punished Hurts for poor ball placement. That competition should benefit both units as the Eagles approach the regular season.

10. Andy Dalton remained first in the QB2 rotation

Dalton received the first repetitions behind Hurts, continuing a pattern the Eagles have maintained despite Tanner McKee 's stronger preseason production.

Dalton badly overthrew Darius Cooper early but recovered to throw a touchdown pass to Elijah Moore .

The depth chart order indicates that the competition remains open. Friday's preseason finale against Cincinnati will provide both quarterbacks with their last game opportunity to influence the decision.

articles.title: Musk's SpaceX to build $100bn launch facility in Louisiana
articles.summary: It will be the firm's biggest site yet and aims to send rockets to space in 2029.
articles.body:
Multi-billionaire Elon Musk's rocket company SpaceX has announced that it will build its largest launch site yet in the southern US state of Louisiana.

Construction of the $100bn (£73bn) project - named Starbase, Louisiana - is due to start next year, with the 125,000-acre (50,585-hectare) site expanding on the company's operations beyond its current Texas headquarters and locations in Florida.

It will be used to "support thousands of Starship flights a year with missions launching to Earth orbit, the Moon, Mars and beyond," SpaceX said on Tuesday.

In June, SpaceX shares started trading on New York's technology-focused Nasdaq in the world's biggest ever stock market debut .

SpaceX said it aims to launch its first Starship flight from the new Louisiana base in 2029.

The facility will add more than 3,000 jobs to the region, the company said .

The Louisiana Economic Development agency said the average wage of workers at the base - the largest of its kind in the world - would be 192% more than the region's current average salary.

It will also create more than 8,100 new jobs indirectly, the agency estimated.

"The historic project will establish Louisiana as a global hub for next-generation aerospace, with the capacity and infrastructure needed to dramatically increase launch frequency and expand access to space," it added.

The facility in Louisiana will share its name with another SpaceX site on the southern tip of Texas.

In 2025, residents in an area of Cameron County, where the company has testing and development operations, approved incorporating the patch of land as a city called Starbase .

Inside the rural Texas town where Elon Musk is basing his business empire

The SpaceX IPO made history. One month on has it lost momentum?

Musk has set out ambitious goals for SpaceX, including plans to reach Mars, develop artificial intelligence (AI) models and launch data centres into space.

In August, SpaceX and Tesla - Musk's electric vehicle and robotics firm - announced plans to build a $16.8bn artificial intelligence (AI) chip making complex in Texas called the Terafab.

The facility aims to meet the companies' growing demand for computing power to support its projects including developing AI and robotics technology over the coming years.

The newly-listed SpaceX is under pressure to convince investors that it will be profitable even as it pursues its expansion plans.

Its shares have tumbled by more than 30% from the highs reached shortly after it began trading but are still higher than their $135 offer price.

articles.title: Watch: US military's 'lethal kinetic strike' destroys suspected drug boat in Caribbean; 4 killed
articles.summary: US News: The US military carried out a strike on a boat suspected of being involved in drug trafficking in the Caribbean Sea on Tuesday, killing four people, a.
articles.body: The US military carried out a strike on a boat suspected of being involved in drug trafficking in the Caribbean Sea on Tuesday, killing four people, as the Trump administration continues its campaign against alleged drug traffickers in Latin America.The US Southern Command posted a video of the operation on X, showing what appeared to be a moving boat followed by a flash after the strike.The military said intelligence had confirmed the vessel was actively involved in drug trafficking, but did not release evidence supporting the claim or provide the identities of those killed.Southern Command said on X, âJoint Task Force Western Hemisphere executed a lethal kinetic strike on a go-fast vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Caribbean. Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel's active involvement in narco-trafficking. The operation killed four narco-terrorists.â It said the vessel was operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Caribbean.The latest attack comes just two days after the US military struck another vessel in the eastern Pacific Ocean, killing two people accused of trafficking drugs.That strike ended a pause of more than two months in the campaign against alleged smugglers.At least 227 killed in boat strikesThe latest attack takes the number of people killed in US military boat strikes to at least 227 in 68 strikes since the Trump administration began targeting suspected traffickers nearly a year ago, according to news agency AP.The military has described those targeted as ânarcoterroristsâ and has said the vessels were operating along known smuggling routes in the Caribbean and the eastern Pacific.However, the military has generally not provided evidence publicly establishing that the targeted vessels were carrying drugs.In Tuesday's case, Southern Command provided no details about the vessel's cargo or the identities of the four people killed.The strikes have faced criticism from human rights organisations, including Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International, as well as independent UN experts, who have described the attacks as unlawful extrajudicial killings, according to Reuters.Trump administration expands anti-cartel campaignPresident Donald Trump has said the US is in âarmed conflictâ with Latin American cartels and has defended the strikes as necessary to stop drugs from reaching the United States and contributing to fatal overdoses.The administration has also sought agreements with Latin American governments to expand military operations against criminal groups on land.War secretary Pete Hegseth said during a visit to Panama this month that Colombia, Guatemala and Honduras had agreed to allow joint US military operations on their territory. Guatemala denied reaching such an agreement, while Ecuador launched similar missions with the US in March.The campaign has drawn scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers and military legal scholars, particularly over the legal basis for the strikes.The Pentagon's inspector general said in May that it planned to examine whether the military followed its established six-phase Joint Targeting Cycle when conducting the strikes.The review, however, was not intended to determine whether the attacks themselves were legally justified.The strikes have also raised questions over their effectiveness, with critics pointing out that fentanyl linked to many fatal US overdoses is generally trafficked over land from Mexico, where it is produced using chemicals imported from China and India.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

Guatemala denied reaching such an agreement, while Ecuador launched similar missions with the US in March.The campaign has drawn scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers and military legal scholars, particularly over the legal basis for the strikes.The Pentagon's inspector general said in May that it planned to examine whether the military followed its established six-phase Joint Targeting Cycle when conducting the strikes.The review, however, was not intended to determine whether the attacks themselves were legally justified.The strikes have also raised questions over their effectiveness, with critics pointing out that fentanyl linked to many fatal US overdoses is generally trafficked over land from Mexico, where it is produced using chemicals imported from China and India.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.body: Khalistani terrorist Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a dual US-Canadian citizen, claimed on Tuesday (local time) that he had been warned by both the FBI and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) of a ânew credible threatâ to his life.Pannun, the general counsel of Sikhs For Justice (SFJ), said FBI agents visited him last Thursday and advised him not to travel until the threat was resolved. He added that the agency asked him to notify them in advance if he did make any travel plans.Also Read | â$100,000 reward for raising Khalistani flags before EU leadersâ: FIR filed against Gurpatwant Singh Pannun ahead of Republic DayâI was warned under the terms of a âDuty to Warnâ law in the United States,â Pannun told the Associated Press, referring to a provision that requires US intelligence and law enforcement agencies to alert individuals when they become aware of credible and specific threats involving murder, serious bodily harm or kidnapping.âIâm not afraid of their death threats. Iâm going to continue, even at the cost of a bullet,â Pannun said.His remarks came after he claimed that the RCMP had also warned him by telephone on Tuesday. Neither law enforcement agency, however, disclosed details of the alleged plot or threat.Pannun further stated that Canadian law enforcement officials had issued similar âDuty to Warnâ advisories to Hardeep Singh Nijjar, another Khalistani terrorist and a Canadian citizen, in the weeks leading up to his assassination in Surrey, Canada, in June 2023.Nijjarâs killing had triggered a major diplomatic row between Canada and India after the then-Justin Trudeau government alleged that the Indian government was involved in the assassination. New Delhi rejected the allegations.In a separate case, Indian national Nikhil Gupta pleaded guilty in February to federal conspiracy charges over a 2023 plot to assassinate Pannun. Gupta is awaiting sentencing, scheduled for November 20, in a Manhattan federal court.Federal sentencing guidelines recommend that Gupta serve at least 20 years in prison.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: As Intelâs CPU market share falls to 31-year low in the market that analysts call 'ugliest segment'
articles.summary: Tech News News: Intelâs share in the x86 CPU market for PCs and servers reportedly fell under 70 percent for the first time ever since the year 1995. According to a r.
articles.body: Intelâs share in the x86 CPU market for PCs and servers reportedly fell under 70 percent for the first time ever since the year 1995. According to a report by Mercury Research, first quoted by CRN, the Intel numbers mark a 31-year low for the semiconductor giant, even as AI spending fueled historic growth for its data center business. Dean McCarron, president of Prescott, Arizona-based CPU-tracking company Mercury Research, confirmed the point about Intelâs 31-year low to CRN in an email following the release of his second-quarter CPU market share report comparing Intel and AMD.Asked to comment, an Intel spokesperson referred CRN to record year-over-year sales growth for its Data Center Group and momentum in its client business unit touted in its latest earnings report as well as a growing number of long-term supply agreements.As per the Mercury report, Intelâs overall x86 CPU market share fell 6.5 points year over year and dropped by under 1 point sequentially to 69.3 percent as AMDâs position grew just as much to 30.7 percent, a new record for the rival, the researcher said.Market share of Intel and AMD in various sub-segments now stands as follows:* Desktop CPU: Intel at 65.1 percent vs. AMD at 34.9 percent* Laptop: Intel at 71.1 percent vs. AMD at 28.9 percentThese figures were based on total CPU shipments for PCs and servers, not including semicustom, embedded and IoT products. If those latter three segments were included, Intelâs share for the second quarter would stand at 65.9 percent, down 4.6 points year over year and down 1.5 points sequentially, against AMDâs 34.1 percent, according to Mercury.One thing that is said to have helped AMD was "better than expected" shipments of the companyâs system-on-chips for gaming consoles. Unlike AMD, Intel does not have a big console business for its chips.Coming back, in the PC market, AMDâs share grew by 6.4 percent year-over-year to a record 30.3 percent against Intelâs 69.7 percent. What also needs to be noted here is that total desktop PC shipments declined by 20 percent year-over-year in the second quarter.How the 'ugliest' segment of the market faredOverall, the report describes the desktop X86 CPU market as "ugly." Hit by limited availability of graphics cards and high prices of components like motherboards, memory modules, and SSDs, the desktop CPU market was particularly weak in the second quarter and shrunk by over 20% year-on-year (YoY) as well as quarter-over-quarter (QoQ) due to seasonality. According to Mercury Research, both AMD and Intel suffered significant annual shipment declines, but AMD all in all held up better.Get the latest technology news and updates. Download the TOI App.
